utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We left off yesterday with this big -- well, big hump of paper and it says "Timetable" and a "Log." Do you consider that this log should have been kept in the Albanian language?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think it should have been kept in the Albanian language because that was the case until before 1990s, as I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: First of all, that's not how it was. And the logbook is kept in Serbian for purposes of transport. What do you think at the railway station in England? Is it kept in English or what language? And in France in French, in Germany in German? What do you think?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's not for the witness. He's given his view about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How, for example, could a controller coming from Belgrade, from the headquarters, how would he be able to control the work going on at the railway station where you were employed? How could he look through the traffic logbook if he didn't know the Albanian language, in a company which was a state-owned company and owned by the State of Serbia, in fact?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: In such cases, either we translate it or the controller from Belgrade, if that was the case, he would have asked a colleague in our department.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I think that's quite sufficient by way of an explanation. I think any reasonable person understands what it means. You said that there was a board in two languages which had been taken down in Urosevac, which is not true. Throughout that time, it always said "Urosevac" and "Ferizaj," the two names. Am I right or am I not?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is pure lie, because since when I worked from 1982 to 1989, it was first "Ferizaj" then "Urosevac." After 1990s, that signboard was removed and then it was written only "Urosevac."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Only the same sign, it said "Urosevac" and "Ferizaj." But let's leave that for a moment. At the entrance to your own village, on both sides there were signs both in Albanian and in Serbian, the name of your village; is that correct? There were name plaques in both languages; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who Njazi Asllani is from your village?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There isn't anyone by this name in my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. He is the registrar in your office. Does that jog your memory perhaps?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There is a Njazi in -- I mean, that was -- used to work in my office, but he's not from our village. He worked there in that office.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But he was an Albanian; is that right? He was working in your village, an Albanian?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did he issue documents to you in the Albanian language or in the Serbian language?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell now, but when I needed to have a document, of course I got it in the Albanian language. Then I never had to have a document, to ask for one, so I don't know. But until 1989, all the documents we used to get in the Albanian language.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about after 1989. Did he issue documents in the Albanian language to you or not?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say anything now because, as I said, I never asked for a document after 1989, so I don't know what he did. But I don't think that they must have been in Albanian language. Probably they must have been in Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But you know whether in those ten years Albanians received documents in the Albanian language or not. Surely you know that. Just say yes or no. I don't mind what your answer is; just give me an answer. That's the easiest possible thing to ascertain. Just say "Yes, they did," or "No, they didn't."

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can testify to what I saw and experienced in my workplace, where the Albanian language was not used. In relation to other documents that you are asking, I cannot testify anything, because I don't deem it necessary to say anything about that here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have now spent half an hour on this question of language, which is completely peripheral, Mr. Milosevic. Let us move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question of language is a basic question, because untruths are being spoken here which claim that there was some sort of discrimination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: In the view of the Trial Chamber, it is a peripheral issue. Now, move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The topic that I haven't exhausted and which was broached by the witness himself is the question of constitutional changes, so I asked what rights were curtailed with these constitutional amendments, to the Albanians and to him. He spoke about language. So was any right curtailed with the advent of these constitutional changes? What did he experience?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You have explored that very fully over the last half hour. Now, you've exhausted the topic. Move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does that mean that there is no other right which he says he lost with the constitutional changes except for the one referring to language?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is the one that he's referred to in his examination-in-chief and your questions must be directed towards it. Now, let's move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that the Albanians who used the Albanian language were deprived of a percentage of their salary. I say that nobody was punished because of that in that way. Do you insist that they were punished? Do you maintain that?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, very much so. We were docked certain shares of our salary. We don't have written statements to prove that, but many people have been punished for using their language, in this case, the Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that means when you received your salary, they would take away out of your hands that percentage and wouldn't give you a slip of paper saying that you were in fact being penalised; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could see the payroll, in which it was reflected that so-and-so was docked his salary, but we haven't kept those papers, because more than a decade has passed. As far as I'm concerned, all my documents were burned, and this happened to many other Albanians, so it was impossible for us to have these papers to show here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't challenge that you can't show documentation, your documents here, but not because they were burned. How come you didn't have any documents, when there was no fire?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He explained that. He said they were burned.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. If that's an explanation that you're satisfied with, then I'm satisfied with that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the written statement which you gave, you said that you were penalised, up to 30 per cent of your salary was deducted, and yesterday you said that your salary was docked up to 50 per cent of your salary. So when is it that you're speaking an untruth?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's not a proper question. It's said that in the statement you referred to 30 per cent, now you refer to 50 per cent. Can you assist us to which of those is right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I didn't say 30 or 50. I only say 15, 1-5 per cent, and up to six months. I said over a period of up to six months. This is what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It says here: "If, for example, an Albanian would write out a ticket for a passenger with the name of the station of departure and destination in the Albanian language, 30 per cent would be deducted from his salary." That is what it says in your written statement, what I read out. Yesterday you said 50 per cent, and that is what it says here on the computer. So one of the two is obviously not true, and I say that both those facts are not true, but you gave two completely different statements. But never mind. We're not only talking about that. You said yesterday, as we're discussing the differences of this kind, you said yesterday that the Serbs set fire to four houses on that particular day, and it says so in exact terms here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Which day are we dealing with?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just find it. Just a moment. Although I assume that you all have this. Just a moment. In the first witness statement, one, two, three, four, five, the sixth paragraph, at the beginning, it says: "On the 5th of April, 1999, at around 9.00, the army, while leaving the village, set fire to two houses which it had previously taken over." That is what it says in the statement. And yesterday your witness, or rather, the witness of this indictment, said that four houses were set on fire. Probably --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, there is a divergence between your statement about the 5th of April when you refer to two houses being set on fire and your evidence yesterday when you said there were four houses. Now, can you clarify that, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can. I don't think it's very important, because that was only the beginning that I said. Then afterwards, many other houses were burned. It may happen that I gave the wrong date about the first four houses that were burned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think that you have some of your own Rules and Regulations and obligations to take measures with respect to false testimony, which is quite obvious here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, Mr. Milosevic. That is a comment. Now, if you've got any other questions of this witness, ask them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course I have. I've just begun.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I did not understand what you actually noticed with respect to the movement of trains, the passage of trains. Yesterday, when you were examined in chief, you said there were some sort of irregular train running, so an extraordinary, irregular train which was not on a regular line according to the timetable and log book, traffic logbook, and so it did not stop at Urosevac. And then you say, according to the timetable, it should have stopped there. Now, my question for you is the following: How could it have -- should have stopped there, according to the timetable, if it wasn't a regular running train on the timetable itself? How do you explain that?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I can explain. If Your Honours allow me, I need a little bit more time, if you think. Please tell me. You give me back the log and I will explain to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness have the exhibit, the log.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let the witness have the original.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's better.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The log is Prosecution Exhibit 63. It was already exhibited yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We took the example of train number 37893. This train is a normal train, a regular train that passes through Ferizaj. When there is -- there are more passengers, they add a "3" number. This is, this train should run according to the regular train. That is, this train should normally have stopped in Ferizaj because that part, "7893," stops. So when we add the "3," it is almost the same train, and it should have stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But it did not stop. So how come? What happened?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It didn't stop because it was full with passengers, and then it left in the direction of Han i Elezit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it didn't stop because there was no room in the train; is that right? It was full?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. It was full.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who decides whether a train is going to stop or not; the stationmaster or the signalman, the dispatcher? Who makes that decision?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Usually the decision can be made by the most important authority for Fushe Kosove, that he should order that the train mustn't stop. But in extraordinary cases, even the dispatcher might do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And in public traffic, urban traffic, when a bus is full, it doesn't stop at a bus-stop, for example. What seems to you to be out of the ordinary there?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: But in the case of train circulation, there isn't such a rule. Please. The train has to stop, no matter if there is room or not. It is a rule. I think everybody should know that. Everybody has taken a train. This is the case everywhere, in the West countries and everywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. The point here is that the stop -- sorry, that the train didn't stop at your station; is that right? Am I to understand what you're saying like that? And you said that when there was no room in the train, when the train was full, then the stationmaster would call the bus company to help with the transport of the passengers. Was that standard practice?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Normally this was not a standard practice. We didn't have such instances before, but that happened that time when people were transported Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. even by trucks, lorries, or by freight carriages, which was not -- which was a very unusual thing. My point was that unusual things kept occurring then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You said that you heard from the priest about the killing of three persons.

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your first statement, you said you heard about it on the 14th. Yesterday, you said you heard about it on the 13th. But at all events, you did not see those bodies, and you did not see anybody actually being killed; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's true that these three killings I didn't see myself, but the fact is that people were killed on the 13th at about 8.00 p.m., and I found out about that on the next day, on the 14th, at about 10.00. It is likewise true that when we did return to the village, we found new dead bodies. Not the three ones that I mentioned earlier but four other persons. They were thrown in a well or a ditch maybe. Then we found the remains of two elderly people who were burned in their homes, who were my neighbours. But the bodies of the three that were killed on the 13th of April, we have never found them to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How come in the written statement you gave you didn't mention these new bodies?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my written statement, which I gave in April 1999, I have mentioned only three people who were killed and four who were taken ransom, hostage. But after our return from -- to the village, we found the bodies of these four people who were taken hostage. And then I can give you even the names of those two who were burned in their own home. And I couldn't give them in my first statement because this -- I found this out when I returned home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you returned home. You mean after the war; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that means that when you returned, you didn't find any fresh bodies that day, but you heard about it when you returned home after the war; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your written statement, you emphasised, in passing but you did write it specifically, that you saw two truckloads of Serb families: men, women, children.

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. I didn't say they were full of people, but I said many -- I said I saw some Serb families getting off the train and coming to Ferizaj. This is the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It says in your statement that you said they were jam-packed, overfull, jam-packed with Serb families.

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what is written there. I know what I said and what the situation was like in reality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, there's an old well-known proverb that when you don't tell the truth, you have to remember minutely what you said beforehand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is that a question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I'm asking whether he knows of that proverb, a proverb to that effect.

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that old proverb, but that does not apply to me. That might apply to you, the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you. I just wanted to know whether you had heard of the proverb. But anyway --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You got the answer. If you ask questions like that, you must expect answers like that. They're not helpful. Now, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you saw Albanians on the move and Serbs on the move, in trains in Urosevac, both Albanian families and Serb families. You claimed that Albanian families were fleeing out of fear from the Serbs. Do you have any assumption as to why the Serb families were fleeing?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know when they went away. What time are you talking about here?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I am talking about these Serb families that you talked about. I'm only talking about what you talked about in your written statement.

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those Serb families didn't leave. They came to Ferizaj, I said. They got off the train and remained in Ferizaj. They didn't leave Ferizaj. I can't tell you from where they came, but it was from the direction of Fushe Kosove maybe, whereas the Albanian families left out of terror exercised against them by the Serb police and army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, according to your testimony, there weren't any such measures in your village except that you had heard that three men had got killed. Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday I was -- we passed very quickly over these events that happened in my village, and I was therefore unable to speak in greater length about what happened then in my village. But since I have the opportunity to answer to your questions, then I can explain to you, if Your Honours allow me, to tell you what real terrible things happened to us during all that time, and the accused can get convinced that it was -- whether it was a right decision to leave the village or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just deal with it briefly.

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the Serb Chetnik forces occupied our village, it was really horrible just to see, to look at them, Distinguished Honours, let alone to have anything to do with them. They were bloodthirsty people. You could see in their eyes their thirst for blood. They kept in their hands knives stained with blood. Only to look at them, it was terrible, let alone to have anything to do with them or to stay with them in the village. Then they started to loot and raid the village all over. First they took away all our vehicles of all the inhabitants of the village and they drove around the village with our own very vehicles, showing off. Then they started to rob us of our money. Every day they came and asked us to give them money, and you had to give them money, because they were armed, and we have given them money. Then our sons, for nine or ten days, dug trenches for them, for those Chetnik forces, and they maltreated them every day. The accused would say that I was not there to see it, but my brother was there, and many other witnesses, who can testify to what these young people went through in the course of their labour for those forces. They were threatened every day that after they finished digging the trenches, they would have to kill them, because this is what they did in Bosnia too, they were telling them. You can imagine yourselves what position we were in at that time, when every day we heard threats that, "You are going to get killed tomorrow."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How come you said none of that yesterday or in any one of your written statements, what you've been saying just now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We need the statements. Can we have the copies, please. There's going to be cross-examination about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. There are two statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: In fairness to the witness, he wasn't asked about this yesterday, but you can ask him, Mr. Milosevic, about the statements. What's said, Mr. Bucaliu, is that there is no mention in your statements of this other maltreatment of villagers by the paramilitaries. Can you help us as to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Distinguished Honours, I may have not said it in my statement, and I don't know how that has come about because I have said all these things even when I was giving the statement. Maybe they haven't written it down because then the statement would have become very lengthy. I don't know. But this is what I said even during the time I gave my statement. I don't know if they have taken down all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. This explanation is sufficient. Let's go back to yesterday, to what you said yesterday. You explained that they had forbidden you any kind of movement in the village except from 7.00 a.m. to 7.00 p.m. and that they told you that at no cost should you leave the village, and you said that you were very frightened. How did you leave, then? How did you leave the village when they had forbidden you to leave the village and when they did not allow you to move around from 7.00 a.m. to 7.00 p.m., only in that period?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained that. On the day that the Chetnik forces came, they showed us the rules of how we could go out from our homes. I said that they told us that we could leave the village only with their own special authorisation, and they had closed both exits to the village. Then a Chetnik called Milja, another called Musa, who were the most active in our village, they told us that, "You cannot leave the village because if the infantry troops of Clinton come to these lands, you will become our shield and you will fight together with us." That is, they wanted to use us as human shields or as cannon fodder, as we say. And this made us even more afraid, fearing that one day they would really mistreat us and use us for that purpose. But we stood there, nevertheless, until after all what we went through, until the first killings came. If the accused denies that, I don't know. He can do what he wishes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I am putting the following question: How did you leave the village if it is true that they had forbidden you to leave the village? How did you manage to leave the village, all of you together, as you had put it?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have explained the way how we managed to leave. I don't want to repeat. If they saw us or not, if they wanted to prevent us or not, I can't say, but we went, as I said, through that valley. Maybe they were not very close, positioned very close to the place from where we left. Maybe they didn't see us leave, because the emptying of the village lasted only 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. That assumption that they did not see you is probably probable. Is it your claim that you did have paramilitaries in the village?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, he said that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who is this Mile person that you've mentioned as somebody I cannot make out? Who is this person? What's his role? Who is this man anyway, this man you've been calling Mile? In all these events, that is.

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mile and Musa were two rabid Chetniks and I know that they were their names. This is all I know. But I also know our neighbour Milan Rudovic was always seen in their headquarters. He was in uniform and kept going to the headquarters of the Chetniks. And he may know better who Mile and Musa were. We couldn't know more than that, than the pseudonyms they used.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who knows better who Mile and Musa were? I did not quite understand what you've been saying.

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The person who may give you better information is my neighbour Milan Rudovic, who was wearing uniform, Serb uniform, and who used to stay with them all the time at their headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you believe these claims? Did you believe that they wanted to use you as a human shield?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we saw what people they were and how they were behaving with us, we believed everything they said, everything bad that they said, with the exception of anything good.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But according to what you said, nobody stopped you, nobody directed you in a certain way, nobody made you go in a certain direction. So is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's right. Just say yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, I need to explain. I just can't say no or yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Bucaliu, we've heard your evidence on the point. It's right, isn't it - you haven't said otherwise - that nobody directed you to go to a particular place when you left the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, nobody told us where to go, but they threatened us at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. We'll get on more quickly if you just answer the questions shortly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You worked in Slovenia as a signalman, and you came to Urosevac in the late 1970s, and then you continued to work as a signalman; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did my school in Slovenia and worked there for one and a half years. Then in 1982, I started to work in Ferizaj train station.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In 1987, you caused an incident when you let a fast train go by and it hit a freight train. There were many injured persons, and you were suspended from work for six months. And then instead of being dismissed altogether, you were returned to work but you got a job as a cashier in the commodities department, and you remained in that position before the war and during the war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's correct that there was an accident in 1987. There were accidents, but this happens everywhere. It's nothing extraordinary that happened. I went even to -- I was taken to police stations and taken to a detention cell, but after that, I was never punished. And that is true that I continued my work for a time as inspector of goods or commodities as then as a cashier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you stayed there all the way up to April or, as it says here, May 1999?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I worked there until 24th -- sorry, until -- yes, on the 24th of March in my workplace, but in the station, I reported until the 14th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know the names of Mahmut Shabani, Muhail Rexhepi, Medi Hoxha [phoen], and Yseni Ysen who worked with you?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were my colleagues. I know them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Precisely at that time these four men reported to Ilic, the trainmaster, and informed him that they had orders from the KLA to go, with the explanation that they would return earlier in that way. However, as opposed to them, I here have a note that you did not report to the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. trainmaster as they did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There are two questions there, two questions there. Do you know about the four men it's alleged having orders from the KLA to go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is ridiculous, distinguished Honours. I can't say anything to testify that -- to that because it is equally true in their case, like it was in my case. That is, we were ordered not to work any more there. It's not true at all what the accused is alleging here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it is your claim that you did not get orders from the KLA to leave the workplace?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There wasn't any KLA in that part where I lived, and I've had never any contacts then with KLA, and I never got any orders from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And do you know Ramadan Muharemi who worked there as well?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was also another colleague.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He also reported to the trainmaster, and he said that due to KLA pressure, he had to leave. He had to sell his house in the centre of Urosevac and to move, because he was not an Albanian, he was a Roma. He did that indeed, and he moved to Subotica where he's been living until the present day, and he can confirm this. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the question? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know Ramadan Muharemi. He was a cleaner in our station and he then worked there. He was in Ferizaj after the war for a long time. Then he why left his house -- it was three or four months after the war. He stayed in the Ferizaj station for only three or four months. I don't know where he is now. If he said that he has left the village for this reason that you are claiming, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that you held meetings at the warehouse of the train station, and when salaries were handed out, you collected money for the KLA? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it correct that you were involved in smuggling foreign exchange, and that is to say, to and from Slovenia, relying on your old connections?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true either. The accused is trying to catch at a straw because he's seeing that he's drowning. So he is saying things here which I don't think matters for this Court either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bucaliu, it's for us to decide what matters. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know a person by the name of Ymer Neziri?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ymer Neziri, yes. He's my neighbour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Together with Ymer Neziri, you participated in the demonstrations of 1981.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. We've been back to 1981 before. We're going to move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not dealing with 1981 in relation to the demonstrations. I want to ask him whether he remembers that together they were breaking windowpanes on the department store called Napredak. That is the department store from Djakovica and Urosevac. And they also took goods from that store, and there is a document to prove that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You are making a series of allegations against this witness which you will have to produce some evidence to support. At the moment, they are pure allegation. We will allow the witness to answer this one and shortly. It's alleged that you were breaking windows in a demonstration in 1981. Were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that at that time I was in Slovenia, in the school. You can say what you want.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. That's the answer. He was Slovenia at the time. Now, let's move on to something more recent and more relevant to the indictment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Everything is related to the indictment, everything that has to do with the witness, and the validity of his statements, the reliability and authenticity of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm not sure we're going to be helped, even if he was breaking windows in 1981, in deciding whether he's telling the truth about events in 1999.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm talking about credibility, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, I'm talking about credibility too. It's a question what is relevant to credibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. The first cousin of witness Bajram Bucaliu, who is also called Bajram, do you remember when he was caught in 1987 at the Bulgarian border and 300 kilogrammes of drugs were found in his van?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the relevance of what his cousin was doing, even if his cousin was doing it? It's totally irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is a well-known fact that the entire family was involved in smuggling tobacco, weapons, and drugs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. You can put that to him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are genuine lies. That's not true at all, that my entire family, or even members of it, were ever engaged in illicit activities or trade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that your father was in prison in Nis because of smuggling?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. I think this is enough. Attempts to smear witnesses do not help the Court. They don't help anybody. If you've got an allegation to make involving the witness's credibility, then you can put it, as you have done, but to start attacking his own family is not relevant.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was just asking questions which relate exclusively to the facts and not to any kind of value judgement, but let's move on from that topic to another area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As the witness explained the reasons which, according to him, were the reason for the departure of citizens from his village to Macedonia, I have the following question: In the neighbouring villages, that is to say, in that area, the neighbouring villages of Talin -- Talinovac [phoen], Nekodim, the village of Varos, Tankosic, Gadnje, Trebno, Plesina, Mirosavlje -- I have been asked by the interpreters to speak more slowly. So the villages of Talinovac [phoen], Nekodim, Varos, Tankosic, Gadnje Trebno, Plesina, Mirosavlje, all of mixed composition, and the village of Rajovica, where the inhabitants are purely Albanian, the inhabitants, throughout the time, remained in their villages; is that true? Is it true that the villagers in all these surrounding villages did not move but stayed in their villages throughout? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about all these villages you enumerated. I knew about the neighbouring villages which were all emptied of people. I said Kamoja [phoen], Sore [phoen], Bibaj, and Varosh. These four villages, they were evicted from Albanians [sic].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: NATO bombed a large storehouse area belonging to your cousin, where your father and brother were employed; is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: NATO had struck that object after we had left the village, because in that place, military forces were deployed, which were there even when we were there, but the bombing came after we left the village. And not only that facility was bombed, but all other facilities. Two tanks were burned and a truck was burned from this bombing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know why a warrant was issued for [indiscernible] Bucaliu, your first cousin?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am Bajram Bucaliu. I don't know what was issued. I don't understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Have you got a first cousin whose name is Brahim Bucaliu, that is to say, your uncle's son on your father's side?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have a cousin called Brahim, and there's another one called Brahim too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to the person who has a house between the railway station and bus station. Have you been able to identify him now?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can identify him, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know why a warrant was issued?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you know -- first of all, do you know if a warrant was issued?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know anything about a warrant. How could I know anything about that? I don't know anything about that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I won't pursue this and go on with my questions relating to that. Does your family own a gas station on the Urosevac-Pristina road?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Not my direct family, but my relatives or cousins do have a gas station. Two cousins, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you work at that gas station yourself?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I work there now at the gas station.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is that a gas station that was built by your cousin Nazmija [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Muhamet, his son. It's his son, Muhamet, who built the gas station.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was the gas station built on the property of a Serb called Milivoj Injic [phoen], on his land?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. He built it on his own property, on property that he had bought with his own money.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the bombing when Bajram Reka's house was hit? And otherwise, next to the house of Bajram Reka, you have a field that you own, so I assume that you know about that.

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around the house of Bajram, there's no land, but I know that the house of Bajram Reka was used as a centre for the Chetniks. Bajram Reka and all his family and all the neighbours were thrown out of their houses. And it was there that the Chetnik staff had their centre. Tanks didn't destroy the house. They were near the building, but the house itself was not. It was the tanks which were burned. The house itself was not touched. And a truck was destroyed from the bombing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know whether anybody fell victim to the bombing? Were there any casualties?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. No Albanians, at least, from our village. As to the forces, the military forces, I don't know. I couldn't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You claim that none of the Albanians at the time were either wounded or injured or killed, that there were no casualties. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true. We weren't there -- the houses weren't bombed. That happened after we left. Everything took place after we left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But when you returned, do you know that all the Serb houses were set fire to except the house belonging to Dragutin Veljkovic [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were burnt. They were all burnt down, both Serb and Albanian houses, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you go, just before the aggression, to the village of Biba at Osman [phoen] and Nabi Biba [phoen] to attend meetings there?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what time you're talking about, but I was an activist of the LDK, and it's possible that I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the meetings that you held, were they in connection with the KLA activities?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We had nothing to do with the KLA. We didn't even know anything about the KLA at the time, and we had nothing to do with their activity, with such activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's go back to the end of your statement, what you said at the end, and your departure for Macedonia. Is it true that in the meantime you went back from Macedonia, back to Urosevac, for short periods, at certain intervals, before you finally went back after the war?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the first day we tried -- on the 15th of April, we tried to cross the border, but we couldn't. When we tried to get to Macedonia on train and were returned to Ferizaj, that's the only time. That's not true what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you: Did you go back now and again? I don't claim that you did; I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not true. I didn't return. I was in Stankovec for about a month, which the accused said didn't exist, but I was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Deal with it shortly, if you would. The answer is you didn't go back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It doesn't matter about the reason. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did anybody take away your documents when you went to Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't take away our documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did anybody direct you to go to Macedonia, tell you to go?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't tell us to go, but we went to Macedonia. We were accompanied by the police, by the police and the army. They didn't say to go to Macedonia, but they accompanied us, escorted us to the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I understood that they drew your attention to the fact that you shouldn't leave the railway line because it was -- that you shouldn't go along the railway line because it was mined and somebody might be killed. Not to go outside the lines.

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what they said. We were afraid. That's what they said, at any rate. I don't know if it was true. So we kept on the rail track. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was undoubtedly true. But do you consider that they helped you in that way or that they were doing something evil towards you by telling you not to leave the railway tracks and not to lose your lives by doing so?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what they were thinking, whether they were trying to save our lives or not. I told you what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking you how you -- what your understanding was of this gesture on their part. How did you understand it?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what I understood. They just said, "Keep on the train tracks." And I know they said that. What they thought, what their reason was, I don't know. We didn't think about that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. As Slobodan Milosevic today brought up the statements himself and presented them to Witness Bucaliu, it will be easier for me to focus on matters which he did not touch upon when asking the witness questions. So let me start off with the list, the list that was brought in and presented as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bucaliu, on the 24th of March, it says that you were not working, as you said. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 24th of March, I was working.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That's why I'm asking you. So on the 24th of March, you were still working. Now, on this list, do you see that half the column has not been filled in and that on that day particularly not half the trains passed by. At least, there were half as many trains as there were the previous day, because four, six, seven trains passed by on that particular day, whereas the previous day many more trains passed by. How do you explain that?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 24th, trains were moving, but on the 25th, there were no trains.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How do you explain that, that after the bombing started, the NATO bombing started, not only did the number of trains not increase, not only was there more in circulation, but on the 24th and 25th of March, on one day there were no trains at all, and on the 24th of March there were half as many trains as usual. How do you explain that? And you said that the number of trains increased.

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible the 24th, 25th, up to the 29th, it's possible that there were no trains. But from the 29th on, there are no -- lots of notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can see here, and I'm looking at it, I have the 29th in front of me and that's where I'll end, the 29th, and then it goes on to the 1st of April, there were trains, and you said, depending on what the last figure was, whether it was an odd number or an even number, that that meant that the train was moving in one direction or in another direction. Now, when the last digit is 0, what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 0 is an even number. It's an even number.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, if you look at the list dated the 29th of March or any other after that date, you will see at that there are about seven, seven trains moving in one direction and seven trains moving in another direction. So the number of trains was equal going to Macedonia and from Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: But that's normal. Every train that goes to Macedonia has to return. They can't all stay in Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All I'm saying is that there were no upsets in the timetable, that everything took place regularly, that trains moved regularly in both directions, as stipulated in the timetable. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So we can understand it, this is -- just a moment. So you're putting that up until the 29th of March or on the 29th of March, the timetable was working normally.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And onwards. It was working normally afterwards too. Trains moved in a regular fashion after that date, going to and from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness's evidence was there were more trains on the 3rd of April. That's the date that he dealt with in his evidence. What is suggested is that you're wrong about that and there were -- the trains were running normally. What is your answer to that suggestion? Less the witness answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can only tell you that the trains up to -- the trains were running regularly. They were going in both directions. And after the beginning of the bombings, there were more trains, and they were exceptional trains running an exceptional -- an exceptional schedule. There were also regular trains, normal trains, but most of them then were irregular trains. That's what I said yesterday. I said there were regular and non-regular trains.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Because you are looking at the date of 29th of March, I don't see any trains in this log between 25th of March to 28th of March. Am I right? Could you check up this matter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you're right. There were no trains from the 25th to the 28th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what I wanted. I wanted to reach the 3rd of April, in fact, and I have it here in my hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If 0 is an even number, as you yourself say, then seven trains left in one direction towards Macedonia and seven trains returned from Macedonia on that day in April. That's what I wanted to hear. I wanted to hear the witness's explanation of that. Nothing changed.

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it changed. I said on the 3rd of April, I told you how they passed through -- how the trains passed through Ferizaj. They didn't stop there except for the train 37897, which stopped in Ferizaj, and the other train that returned from Elez Hani. Aside from that, all the other trains just passed through Ferizaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No. My question wasn't that. Yes, I know. You explained that. You explained that. All I'm doing is noting that you said that nothing changed. There were no irregular trains. Seven regular trains went in one direction, and according to the timetable, they returned from the opposite direction as the timetable states.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: His whole evidence is that the trains were irregular. That's the whole point of his evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's why I'm asking, Mr. May -- Judge May. That's what I'm asking, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Why are you challenging it? What is the basis of your challenge to this evidence which he's given?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not challenging it. All I'm doing is saying that I think the documents show that for the most part everything ran regularly, that a certain number of trains run in one direction, a certain number of trains ran in the opposite direction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... more quickly. We'll ask the witness. Were the trains running regularly that day or not, according to the document which you have in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we're talking about this date -- there's a lot of dates, but let's take this one here. According to the list, there is no regular train. They are all irregular trains. According to the numbers we have here, you can see that they are irregular trains.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I won't pursue the matter. I think there is a logic that has to be applied, but I'll leave it to the Trial Chamber to assess.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What I wanted to ask in connection with everything that was said here with respect to the events at the railway station, I won't go back to the language problem, the language issues, but in your previous statement, that is to say, in your statement dated the 16th of -- no, the 29th of August, 2001, you said that the money fines were prescribed generally because for the train tickets, the name of "Urosevac," the place, was written in the Albanian language, "Ferizaj," as the ultimate destination; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said there were times when it was -- it was questioned why was it written "Han i Elezit" on the ticket. A friend of mine was punished for that because he wrote it "Han i Elezit."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you something else in fact. You work at the railways, in the railways, and you've been working there for many years. You know the problems that existed. When you leave Kosovo, it's not a large, a great distance. When you leave Kosovo -- the Albanians travelled a great deal. They went to Bosnia and Montenegro, passed through Serbia on their way to third countries, and they used that main road a lot through Croatia. And you know that very often there were problems on the railway lines, at railway stations, that when you write "Ferizaj" most people, not in Kosovo but further on in Yugoslavia, which existed until 1990, that there were problems because they couldn't tell where the people had -- where the point of departure was for these passengers, that they were even asked to leave the trains because of that. Is that true? Did you know about that problem?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that. There may have been certain problems. I think the inhabitants of Yugoslavia itself didn't have any problems whereas people abroad, from abroad, might have had a problem with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me now go on to the statement. Slobodan Milosevic has focused on the statement. But I should just like the witness to explain one point. He said on the 2nd of April, when the army arrived, when the army came to your village, Witness, and you explained that there was an officer, that you had a conversation with him, but in your statement, you told the investigators that, "The officer had said that they were the regular army and that we should not flee." Was that it? Is that what he told you, that you shouldn't flee because they were the regular army? Is that what he said to you and is that what you've said in the statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, so that we can follow your examination, will you tell us where this is; which statement and where we can find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The statement is dated the 24th and 25th of April. It is his first statement given in 1999. And on page 1, paragraph 4 is what I'm referring to. In the English version, the one you have, that is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is that correct, that he said, "We are the regular army, and you needn't flee"?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. That's what he said. But later, we found out that that was not the case at all. He did say that. He said, "There's no reason to leave. We are the army. Don't be afraid of us." That's what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But you also said over the past two days that you left but that nobody told you to leave, that nobody demanded that you leave.

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We stayed in the village for several days after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And then you decided to leave the village?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on the 14th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we come to your second statement, dated the 16th of June, and the English version -- in the English version, it is on page 4. Page 4. And the date is the 15th of April, the date that is mentioned. And you say, "That first morning, the 15th of April, 1999, once again at the railway station I saw the police." Is that right? Is that what you said? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Next you go on to say, "They were looking at what was going on and tried to introduce a certain amount of law and order." Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't think they were -- say that they were trying to introduce law and order. I didn't see anything particular. I was just there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That's what it says in your statement.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters apologise, but they haven't got a copy of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right, but what is important is the following. You say: "At the station, there were about ten policemen. I didn't notice whether they were preventing people or directing people in which direction to go." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't tell anyone where to go. They -- people were leaving. It didn't matter where they went.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Two paragraphs lower down -- so they didn't address you in any way or make any suggestions to you, did they?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at the station in Ferizaj, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, two paragraphs further down, you state the following --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you. It's now a minute past 11.00. Are you going to be many minutes longer?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two more minutes. Two more minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Two paragraphs lower down, you state the following: Vule, you mentioned Vule. Who is Vule?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vule was the station head at Han i Elezit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you said: "Vule offered to see my family and myself off to the border, to escort me, together with the policemen, but I didn't take up his offer." So he offered to transfer -- transport you and your family, but you didn't accept the offer because it wouldn't have been honourable for you to leave your fellow villagers; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true, because the station head at Elez Han, after the first day when we couldn't get across the border into Macedonia, offered to help me and my family, but because I was with all the other people who were in the train, I didn't want to accept the offer to cross the border just with my family. And then the next day, we tried and got across.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge May, with the Court's indulgence, I wanted to clear up one more matter, and it is to be found on paragraph 3 of the second statement, on page 1. After the break, may I be allowed to clarify one more point, after the break, in that second statement of his?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll adjourn now for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I just want to draw your attention to the third paragraph in the second statement, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bajram, earlier on you said that all the way up to 1998, you did not support the KLA.

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, because at the beginning the KLA was something which I knew nothing about, so how could I respect it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Also you said then: "I thought I could not do anything against Serbia, and I knew that it would be hard to achieve anything without some help from outside the country."

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is what I thought then, because having to deal with such a major military force like Serbia was, I would normally think that we would suffer great consequences.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You said that, "When the bombing started, I changed my position." What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may coincide with the bombing, but when I saw what one man -- one human being can do to another human being, from what I saw happen in my village, it was but normal and clear to all of us that if you -- that if we sat cross-legged, we would be killed just the same. Then I had to change my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Before I put another question to you, let me ask you the following: Once, as you said, you helped a KLA soldier when the unit withdrew due to the presence of strong Serbian forces. In which way did you help him?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a great offensive of the Serb forces against the KLA positions in the Sharre Mountains, and the KLA had withdrawn. In so doing, the son of a colleague of mine happened to be left behind in the village, and my colleague asked me to help him, to transfer him from -- to take him to another place.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How big was this unit that was retreating? How many men were there in that unit?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no information about their number. I can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you know whether before the bombing and after the bombing there were clashes between the KLA and the army and the police of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about that after I read in the information media. Yes, there were clashes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm just asking you the following. That's why I've been asking you all these other questions. Due to these clashes between the KLA - I mean before the bombing and after the bombing - did that lead to the withdrawal of the population, either Serb or Albania, from these areas where the fighting was taking place?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not true. It's not that it was because of the NATO bombing that we left the village, either we Albanians or Serbs. The Albanians left because of the tragedy perpetrated against them by the Serbs, while the Serbs stayed there and didn't leave. I can testify to this in several ways. I may tell you -- I may cite only an example when I was in town and the alarm went off about -- for the NATO airstrike, and I could see the Albanians, that none of them left the town because they thought that NATO doesn't shoot at the civilians, doesn't strike at the civilians, and that was the case, while the Serbs left. They tried to find shelter in cellars, in other secure places.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You said in your statement here - I don't want to show it to you yet again - that you and all your people gathered together during the bombing in one house. While the bombing lasted, that is.

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We got together in a house. Not because of the bombing but because we felt safer in the face of the Chetnik forces who were in the village. Because if it were for the bombing, there were no place we could go because there wasn't any shelter for us. But the fact is that we felt so secure, so safe that only the fact that when bombing started on the 24th of March it was a great joy for us because it was there that we saw our salvation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: There were power cuts often from the 24th onwards. That's the way you had put it as well.

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The power was cut at about 8.00 p.m. and came -- was released in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you one more thing. Did this have anything to do with the bombing?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this was so to make it easier for the Chetnik military forces to do what they intended in the night, to circulate freely without being seen. And this is what happened, because the people, the three people, were killed precisely when the power was cut, Emin Zeka and his two sons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This happened every evening? The first five or six days, the way you had put it.

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the time I was in the village, this is what happened. The power was cut off every night.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, two areas just.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Mr. Bucaliu, on cross-examination you were asked about the 2nd of April when the army came to your village and they told you that they were the regular army and that you should not flee. But you continued saying that it changed after. What changed?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That situation changed because that army, which described itself as a regular army, started to burn our homes, to raid and loot. So the very army that told us not to be afraid started to do all these things. So they didn't suit action to words.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Mr. Bucaliu, did you see them burning the houses, and did you see them looting?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw them burning the houses. As to the looting, I can give my own example. They took away my car, my tractor, and so.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Thank you. Also on cross-examination, you answered that you decided to leave on the 14th of April. Did you want to leave?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if there is anyone in the world to wish to leave his own property, home, everything at the mercy of such Chetniks and to leave his home and his fatherland. If there is someone to think that, to leave his home and go to an unknown destination, I don't think that this can happen. But for us, it was important to save our lives. We didn't feel any pains at leaving behind all our properties. The only concern for us was to save our lives.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: So was there any particular moment or particular fact that made you decide that you were leaving at that moment?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I said during my testimony, apart from various acts of maltreatment, looting and raiding, they started to kill people. That did it, when we heard that people were starting to get killed. Then we decided to leave, because we were afraid that the same thing might happen to us. And this is shown by the people who were left behind, Fehmi Hoxha and his wife, my first cousin, who we found only their remains, when we returned, in their burned house.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Mr. Bucaliu, that applies also to the other people that left with you; do you know if that was the same -- they would have the same fear as you had?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. It was normal for all of them to feel the same thing. When we start to hear that people began to be killed, nobody had anything to say. It was chaos. It was confusion prevailing among all of us. We didn't know where to go. It was quite spontaneous when we started to flee the village on -- through the road that I always -- already explained to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bucaliu.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: No more further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Bucaliu, so I can be clear about this question of the regularity of the movement of the trains, I'd like the usher to give you the logbook and for you to look at each day from the 24th of March until the 3rd of April. And I'd like you to comment on the question of the movement of the trains on each day; how many trains there were, whether the trains were full, matters of that kind which are relevant to the question of the regularity of the movement of the trains. So each day from the 24th of March.

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said earlier --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you please put the log on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you now looking at the 24th?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the 24th March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How many trains were there that day?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 24th of March, there were seven trains running: three in one direction, apparently four in the opposite direction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And what is your evidence - remind me - as to the average number of trains each day?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The average number was six: three in one direction, three in the opposite. That was the regular schedule. Six trains over 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So on the 24th, we had three and four. And were the trains full, are you able to say, on the 24th?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 24th, I don't think they were full, because I was at work, and the trains had only two carriages each and were not full. But after the 24th of March --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The next day now, the 25th, and give us the same information on the 25th.

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 25th of March -- there are no notes until the 29th of March. If I may continue from 29th onwards --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Until the 29th, there's no record in your logbook of the movements of the trains?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there isn't any.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Why is that?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be sure why that is, but probably the trains didn't run. I can't remember precisely this particular time, but this is what can be inferred from the log.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move to the 29th, then, the next day when you have information. How many trains were there on the 29th?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 29th, there was only one train. It has come up to Ferizaj station and has returned, from what I see in the log.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Any indication as to how many passengers were in that train?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: There isn't any indication as to the number of passengers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's move to the 30th.

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 30th, there were two trains, I see here. On the 31st, there were more trains.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. Just -- we haven't finished with the 30th. Two trains in each direction or just one direction?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: One in the direction of Ferizaj, one in the direction of Fushe Kosove; opposite.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. And the 31st?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 31st, there were eight trains; four in one direction and four in the opposite direction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And any indication as to the capacity, the number of passengers?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Unfortunately, no, I don't see any records here about the number of passengers. As you can see, there are records only about the number of trains that passed through. As to the number of passengers, this is taken down at the departure station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's move to the 1st.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. In terms of a capacity problem, I'd like to clarify this matter. You testified that the reason the train did not make a stop at Ferizaj station, you explained the reason as being due to the fact that the train was full; is it right?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. When I was there, I saw such trains passing by and not stopping, and they were full of travellers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
