utterances.text: According to this log, not only the trains with odd numbers, but those with even numbers didn't make a stop at Ferizaj station. Does that mean that trains from the border were also full?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: In very rare cases they have been full, as the case was with our train when we returned back from the border to Ferizaj station. But in other cases, the trains that went were full; when they returned, they were empty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But also some empty trains did not make a stop at Ferizaj station; am I right?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When they returned from Han i Elezit to Ferizaj, they were empty. Sometimes they did not stop, from what I see in the log.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's continue. I think we were at the 1st of March -- 1st of April, rather, 1st of April. How many trains were there on the 1st of April?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 1st of April, there were seven trains.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Give us the breakdown as to the direction. How many in the direction of the border, going to the border?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Four went to the border direction, three returned from Han i Elezit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And is there an indication as to the capacity?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there isn't any indication as to the capacity. Unfortunately, no such records are ever kept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: 2nd of April.

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 2nd of April, there were 13 trains.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And give us the breakdown as to the direction. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Seven in the direction of Han i Elezit and six in the opposite direction, from the border to Fushe Kosove.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, can you tell by looking at the log whether these were regular or irregular trains?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of the number of the trains I see here, all these trains were irregular trains, I mean not normal trains, and from the log, not regular -- not a single regular train has run. All have been irregular trains.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Did they stop at Ferizaj or not?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 2nd of April, only train with number 14395 [as interpreted] stopped. It came to Ferizaj at 6.08 and left at 15 [as interpreted]. The other trains didn't stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And how can you tell that they didn't stop?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell from this arrow that you see here, which shows that it has only passed through the station. The train that stops, you see a mark the time when it has arrived, how long it has stopped, and when it has left the station. So this train 4935 [as interpreted] has come at 6.08 and has left at 7.15. And you can see the same with other trains have not stopped at Ferizaj, and we come at another train here that has stopped, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And is the situation the same as to the capacity; you are not able to say whether the trains were full on that day, the 2nd?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't keep a diary for every day, but most of the time that I was there, and I saw with my own eyes, the trains were full of people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. On the 3rd, the last day now, the 3rd of April, how many trains were there?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 3rd of April, there were 16 trains.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How many in the direction of the border?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Seven towards the border.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Isn't it 14? Could you count it again?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, 14. You're right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did they stop at Ferizaj?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only the train number 37897 stopped at Ferizaj, and the other one from the border stopped at 1456, 1458. The other trains didn't stop at Ferizaj at all. There, at the bottom, you can see trains stopping at Ferizaj, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Were they regular trains?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, none of them were regular trains.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Did the trains normally stop at Ferizaj?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Ferizaj station is one of the largest stations, and all major trains, all international trains, always stopped in Ferizaj. All passengers trains stopped, because it's one of the biggest stations in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Bucaliu, that concludes your evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One thing was not done, Your Honours. These two statements that were made by the witness to the investigator, they did not receive a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. They will be exhibited.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Witness statement dated 24, 25 April 1999, will be Prosecution Exhibit 64, and the next one Prosecution Exhibit 65.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Now, what is it, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume that I have the right to an additional question with respect to what has been said so far after my cross-examination, the re-examination. Do I have that right or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. No, you can't have another question. The only question you could ask would arise from the questions which the Judges ask. If you want to ask anything about the train timetable, you could.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only on the basis of what the Judges asked; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, about the train timetable.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About what Judge Robinson asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, you can ask about.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We just heard the witness answer that on the 25th, 26th 27th, 28th there were no trains and that on the 29th there was just one train which arrived at Urosevac and returned, went back. That means that for practically five days there was no communication and traffic towards Djeneral Jankovic. And then the next five days are taken, of which the first two days was regular traffic and in the following three days, it was doubled. Now, if we make an average for the first five days in which there was no traffic and the next five days in which traffic was increased, can we note there that, on an average, there was a regular number of trains running over a period of ten days. Because if there are no trains five days, then it is quite normal that over the next five days, traffic is increased. Can we draw that observation? Can we take note of that? That is my question. Is that what we are able to conclude?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, that is a comment. The witness has given his evidence about the number of trains and you can address us on it and on the average. Now, Mr. Bucaliu, thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give your evidence. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No more questions. No, Mr. Tapuskovic. The witness has been here long enough and answered enough questions. Yes. You're free to go. Let the original of that document be given to the Court. The witness can go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Patrick Ball, please. The Chamber has his report. I don't think it yet has his curriculum vitae. I'm not sure about that. It has a supplement to his report, or an addendum. Your Honour, I'm proposing to take the report shortly but to explain it in terms that are comprehensible to non-experts, and I hope that's an acceptable course.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There is a way to address a Court, Mr. Tapuskovic, which you should bear in mind. Yes. Let the Senior --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the Senior Legal Officer come up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, I was on my feet. I didn't think you saw me on my feet. Before Patrick Ball comes in, as the amicus curiae, we decided to set forth certain matters in respect of that. So my I please have several minutes during which I can set forward some of our positions with respect to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just keep the witness out for a moment, please. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I want to say is the following: We first of all have to clear up the status that the next report entitled Killings and Refugee Flow in Kosovo, March to June 1999, and it is dated the 3rd of January. Patrick Ball has the status of an expert witness. Now, during disclosure and all the addendums, the Prosecution refers to Rule 94 bis. That means that it acts according to Rule 94 bis, and the report plus the additions may be considered as expert evidence. I agree with the President of the Chamber, presented two days ago, that the report can be read and should be read by at least two members of the amicus curiae. I read it on time. I have my assistant, and I have become well-acquainted with the report when it was disclosed, since the very beginning. However, that is not what I want to bring up here, whether the amici have read the report or not or which language. But what we're discussing here is the accused and his guaranteed minimum rights, according to Article 21 of the Statute, and one of these rights is to provide the accused enough time to prepare for his defence. For the first time, the report of Mr. Ball, in the English language, was served on the 18th of January, 2001, to both the accused and the amicus curiae. This disclosure of the material and the report, with some exceptions, was performed simultaneously. We took that. Then we received another copy of that same report in English and became acquainted with it. In its lists, the Prosecution, with respect to the order of witnesses dated the 7th of February and the 8th of February, indicated to us that the translation would be disclosed on the 18th of February 2002, but it was disclosed three weeks late, exactly three weeks late. The Rule is, Rule 94 bis and the amended Rule of the 20th of December, 2001, when on the 6th of March when we were given an addition, provides for the fact that expert witness reports should be disclosed within a time limit prescribed by the Trial Chamber or by the Pre-Trial Judge. This Trial Chamber, on the 11th of January, issued an order confirming the oral orders given from the pre-Status Conference on the 9th of January, and it was decision number 4 or order number 4 which states the following, and I'm going to read it out word-for-word: "Written statements by all witnesses who are to testify in person must be disclosed to the accused in a language which he understands before the beginning of trial. The witness whose report has not been disclosed in this way can be called exclusively with permission by the trial -- pre-trial Chamber." That is what the order states. After a request made by the Prosecution after the 18th of January, the Trial Chamber changed its order of the 11th of January. Therefore, after that, at the request of the Prosecution on the 18th of January, the Chamber changed its order dated the 11th of January, extended the time limit for disclosure, and in point 3 of that order, of the order of your Trial Chamber, it states that the accused and the amicus curiae should make maximum time of the time disposal and prepare for cross-examination of these witnesses, although the Trial Chamber, at the trial, will take into consideration all demands and requests for deferring cross-examination because of insufficient time for preparation. That was your own decision. And the report of expert Ball is very complex. It requires knowledge of the material in hand and methodology. As the amicus curiae and the obligations entrusted to us, I wanted to draw your attention to these circumstances to ensure a fair trial for the accused, and we therefore consider the Trial Chamber should assess whether disclosure was conducted in keeping with the Rules and Regulations and whether it is in keeping with the time limits prescribed. If the Trial Chamber decides that disclosure in the language understood by the accused was done within the stipulated time limit, we are of the opinion that the position of the accused set out on the 11th of March towards the end of the day at trial, when he said he didn't have enough time to prepare for this expert witness, namely Mr. Patrick Ball, that there was reason enough to defer cross-examination as you yourself provided for in your order dated the 21st of January, 2002. Thank you. And I apologise, Judge May, for the misunderstanding a moment ago. I really was on my feet because I didn't think you had seen me standing. Those, then, are our reasons and our position. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The report was disclosed in accordance with the Rules in English on several occasions. It was on 18th of January first, on the 6th of March second. I can deal with the addendums and appendices and matters of that sort which have different dates. The B/C/S was forecast as being available at an earlier date than in the event CLSS were able to provide, but it was certainly provided at the first available opportunity. The material has been available for the accused to read by himself or his associates, and in our respectful submission, the evidence should be taken not just in chief with deferred cross-examination but in full now. What I propose to do is to go through, as I've already suggested, the report in a way that will make its concepts understandable by the lay observer, reader, or listener, and it may be that any question of deferment could be considered at the end of the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll hear the evidence in chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The witness can come in, please. It may be the Chamber, before the contribution from Mr. Tapuskovic, was checking on the documents it had before it, which is the report itself, and then there's the addendum, which is a three-page document, I think, and the curriculum vitae, which I think you don't have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Full name, please.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: My name is Patrick Ball.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I propose, rather than going slavishly through a curriculum vitae, with the Court's leave to produce as an exhibit his curriculum vitae, simply to ask him a couple of questions about his background, if that would be acceptable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Curriculum vitae, then.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 66.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Dr. Ball, you, I think, have university degrees, ultimately a Ph.D. in Sociology.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sociology, including matters of statistics? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Have you, in the course of passing those various exams, which are set out in the curriculum vitae, used statistics?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes, quite a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And for the last how many years have you been full-time engaged in working as a statistician?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Full time since 1997, I think all of my work has been quantitative and analytical. Quite a bit before that, but not full time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Have you, for some years, focused on human rights events and the application of disciplines of sociology and, in particular, statistics, to those events?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes, since 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And so if we look - and this comes on the fourth and fifth pages, I think, of your curriculum vitae, fifth and sixth - working in reverse order, have you worked on projects in Sri Lanka; Kosovo; Guatemala; South Africa, for the Truth and Reconciliation Commission; Haiti; Guatemala again; Ethiopia, two projects, I think; and El Salvador?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Dr. Ball, in the course of working for human rights events as a statistician, did you develop something of a relationship with the organisation Human Rights Watch?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And did you find yourself lecturing them or addressing courses in some way from time to time?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: I give talks at Human Rights Watch offices in New York and Washington, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And in the course of your lectures to them, did you focus on something, perhaps a bit of an obsession or a bee in your bonnet?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: I often spoke about the difficulty of understanding a massive phenomenon with purely qualitative methods; that is, if the human rights event being studied has more people involved than you can easily interview, then perhaps statistical methods would assist an understanding of.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And does that explain how you first became involved in the Kosovo project --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- at least for the preparation of this report?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did Human Rights Watch get in touch with you in April of 1999?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: First in March of 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: March of 1999.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Inviting you to do what and to go where?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: They asked me to assist them in the field, perhaps to design my own project, not a Human Rights Watch project, but they saw the need for a project like the ones I had done in the other countries you had listed. So they invited me to accompany them to Albania to design such a project.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to remember, Dr. Ball, to leave a gap between your answer and my question, because as we are speaking the same language, there's the risk that we will overtax the interpreters otherwise.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you go to Kosovo, and in particular, to a border point in the south-west?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: I went to Albania, actually, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry, yes, to Albania.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes. And then to a border point in northern Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Which is on the south-west of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When there, did you notice something about the method or methods of recording events that was going on?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes. There were two methods by which refugees were being counted as they crossed the border from Kosovo into Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Two different methods, being what?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: The first were registries prepared by the Albanian border guards. They had developed a form on which they attempted to register the name, or the surname, the year of birth, the place of residence or location, and the quantity of each party or group that crossed the border from Kosovo into Albania. That was the first method.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The second?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: The second were teams of observers from UNHCR and the OSCE, or former OSCE mission in Kosovo, who maintained head counts with mechanical hand-held counters that they reported to UNHCR, I believe in Kukes, the Albanian town some distance from the border, a few kilometres, and then those were recorded in daily press reports in Tirana.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: To a statistician, is there any significance or value in matters being recorded not in one way but in two or more?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes. Having two measurements of the same thing is enormously valuable because we can compare the two and determine how they might differ, and then if they differ, which might be more important, reliable, or sound.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And I'll take the story comparatively swiftly and then get to the report. Did you return to America to seek initial funding for a project and did you obtain funding from, I think, the Ford Foundation?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes. I returned to America --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If it's yes, yes will do.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll deal with how you obtained some of the records, in any event, when you were back at the border crossing shortly, but I just want to conclude the question of funding. Were there earlier publications by you or by you and others in relation to the work you did, publicly available?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Earlier than the current report.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, earlier than this report.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes. There were two.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were they funded by the Ford Foundation or were they funded by the second funder, to whom we'll turn?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: The first report, entitled "Policy or Panic?" was published in March of 2000 and was funded by the Ford Foundation and the John D. and Catherine T. MacArthur Foundation and the Institute for Civil Society, all American private foundations. The second report, published in September of 2000, entitled "Political Killings in Kosovo," was published with the American Bar Association and Central and East European Law Initiative, and it was funded by funds provided to ABA/CEELI by the US government.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And is that the funding that leads to the report that's before this Court --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- today?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you make any presentations to the United States funders?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One or more than one?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: I made one presentation in July 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you have any further contact with the United States funders other than that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's go back, then, to your return to the border once you had started the process of obtaining funding for the project, and you can deal with this very shortly, I think. Did there come a time when it was not possible to go with safety to the border point, where you believe records to have been?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes. When I returned to the border in early June 1999, the border post had been fired upon a few days previously. A journalist had been seriously hurt and the border guards decided to withdraw several hundred metres into Albania, to a point where they believed they would be safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: To cut this long story short, I think you believe the records to be in the border post, or some of them.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Eventually you went to the border post yourself.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes, I did, personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: With an accompanying guard. Did you find some records?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Which type of records did you find? Did you find the first type or the second type that resulted from the clickers?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: I found the border guards' registry forms.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And did you gather those up --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- bring them back, and use them as part of your source material?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we now move to the report itself, at that early stage, was there any divergence between the total numbers of people moving that you can tell us about at that post?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Divergence --?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In numbers, at that early stage.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: After we had obtained the records and keyed them into a database, we looked at the number of people reported each day crossing the border and compared the numbers reported by UNHCR to the numbers reported by the border guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So this is right at the beginning, raw material?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did the figures differ, and if so, what was each?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: They differed on some days, and all of the days on which they differed were days of very heavy flow over the border. And in every difference, the registries by the border guards were fewer; they were smaller numbers than the UNHCR figures.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the two different figures were?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: The total figures that there were 272.000 people registered by the border guards, and four hundred, four thousand [sic] people registered in the UNHCR daily counts reported in their daily press reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So the clickers reported more than the handwritten records?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to ask that the report that has already been made available should become an exhibit, and I'm proposing in due course that we might use a version of the report which I've got here, page by page laid on the overhead projector so that those listening and watching can understand the points we're making. But first of all, may the report become an exhibit, Exhibit 67.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm afraid not every page is numbered, because the first thing I want to look at, very briefly, is the Scholarly Review Panel, which comes two pages after the last numbered page, page 69.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 67.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And if the usher would be so good, what we can do with our loose-leafed version is make available to the usher - it might be easier that way - pages to which I'm referring, and then he can display them. It's two pages after 69, the Scholarly Review Panel. If that could just go on the ELMO, please, the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You'll see that on the screen in front of you. Did you, in accordance with -- well, you must tell us if it's in accordance with practice. Did you submit drafts of the report that's been produced to a scholarly review panel?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is that standard practice for reports of this general kind or not?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: This is a bit more rigorous than reports submitted to non-expert groups. Things that are published in professional journals are reviewed according to a standard and formal process. Since we were submitting this to the Office of the Prosecutor, we had to create a panel of reviewers who could give this equally rigorous review.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did they review it on two occasions?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: They did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At each review, did you receive advice as to further steps to be taken, further elements to be introduced into the report?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And we see listed various names: Dr. Helge Brunborg, Dr. Ronald Lee, and Dr. Francoise Seillier-Moiseiwitsch, the first three. Do any of those occupy particularly senior positions in the world of statistics?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: I consider that all three of them occupy senior positions. Dr. Brunborg formerly worked for the Office of the Prosecutor here and is very well regarded in international demography, in addition to his --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, that's enough for these purposes. Dr. Ronald Lee?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Was formerly President of the Population Association of America, the Professional Association of Demographers in the United States.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then Dr. Francoise Seillier-Moiseiwitsch?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: She is the chair of the Human Rights Committee of the American Statistical Association.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, that's all I need to ask. Others can ask about other names if necessary. Just this: At any stage in the review process, did you either reject the advice you were given by the panel or did the panel ever challenge your conclusions as unacceptable or in any doubt?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is that no to both?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: That's no to both. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let's go to the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Earlier the witness said that since he was submitting the report to the Office of the Prosecutor, I wanted to find out whether the report was commissioned by the Office of the Prosecutor or whether it was done independently and then submitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you give us the history of that? You've already told us that your earlier two reports or the two earlier reports with which you were associated were published publicly. Just explain how it was that you were involved with the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: After I completed each of the previous two reports, before they were made public, I came to The Hague and gave brief presentations to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. people here at the Tribunal, covering the basic findings of the report. On that basis, I was asked by people in the Office of the Prosecutor if this evidence would be sufficient to go -- to bring before the Court, and I answered that, in order to bring it before the Court, it should be done with additional data and in an even more rigorous fashion. They assisted me, negotiating with the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe for a third source of information, and they provided me, the Office of the Prosecutor provided me with a database of exhumation records based on the fieldwork of the exhumation teams. At no time did the Office of the Prosecutor suggest findings or suggest what I should conclude. They did ask me to do this with the highest scientific standards, and they emphasised the importance of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We're going to see some of these matters reflected at two places in the evidence in the course of the morning or the early afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we turn to looking at particular pages of the report and in order to have exhibits in good order, can we produce one exhibit that's outside the report, which is an example of the record you took from the border crossing point, which I think was Morina, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 68.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Which I think has a translation with it. If the original can go onto the overhead projector. And the -- if the original could go onto the overhead projector - thank you very much - briefly so those viewing can see it. And then having been viewed, if the original can go -- well, no. We can now look at the translation, putting that on the overhead projector in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you just tell us, please, Dr. Ball, what this particular page is.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: This is one of the 690 pages that I recovered from the border post at Morina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And it shows, in respect of individuals, their name, their address - that is the address from which they had come - their year of birth, and what does the last column help us with? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: That's the total number of people in their group that crossed the border with them. Only the name of the head of household or head of the party was registered.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So that name number one from Suhareke, 27 people in that party, is that what you're saying? It says "Tool type" I see on the translation, but --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: I don't think it's "Tool type." Yes, that's what it means.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. I think it will be helpful if we go first of all to a first graph which we can find on page 5 of the report, and then we'll come back a few pages to fill in a few blanks, but let's go to page 5 first of all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We have both text and the graph, but I'd like the unit, if it can, to focus on the graph, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is one of many graphs that we're going to be looking at. This is -- or several, not many. This is an "Estimated total refugee flow over time," and in the vertical axis it's "People leaving their homes," and we can see the dates concerned moving along the bottom. Yes. Now, this particular graph, was this a graph simply drawn from the raw material that you were able to collect? We'll discover what sources of raw material you had in due course, but yes or no, was this a graph that was provided from raw material?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right. What was it, then?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: The raw material consisted of the border records we discussed earlier, supplemented by the UNHCR reports and a number of other smaller sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Am I or am I not using the word "raw material" correctly? You had other sources.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll identify them in due course. Having various sources of material, you then read from the material whether someone's left their home in the period 24th of March, 25th of March, 26th of March, and so on.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You total up the figures from all sources, making such allowances for duplication as you have to, and then you've got this particular graph.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: We also corrected for the time it takes people to travel to the border --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: -- from their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll come to all those details in a minute. Yes.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: With that clarification, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Right. To a statistician and perhaps to anybody, is there a characteristic in this particular graph?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Namely?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: There seem to be three quite distinct phases or points at which refugee flow is high. First, the flow rises to high points during late March and early April. Then this declines to a relatively much lower point. It rises again to a peak in mid-April, subsequently declining to a low point in later April. Then toward the end of April and early May, it rises in a series of small peaks, finally declining toward near zero for the remainder of the period.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So three peaks, as it were, and two troughs?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We're going to see something similar in other graphs a little later, but immediately what does that shape suggest when contrasted with, for example, the possible assertion that there was a constant cause causing people to become refugees in the way suggested by the line?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: This pattern would not be characteristic of a constant cause. The stop-and-start pattern of the peaks and troughs suggests more strongly a cause that itself started and stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, again we'll break this down in due course into a little bit more detail, but did you from some stage then in the project, once you became aware of these peaks and troughs, consider three possibilities as causes or possible causes for peaks and indeed troughs?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Having seen this graph and others with this characteristic pattern of peaks and troughs, we concluded that there must be some cause. Accordingly, we considered three possible causes that might account for this peak and trough pattern.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Namely?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Those were, first, that KLA activity, in particular clashes with Serb forces, could be a cause; second, that NATO airstrikes might have been a cause; and third, that Yugoslav force activity might have been a cause.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At the end of the exercise, when we reach your conclusions, in general - just yes or no - is it possible to identify causes or is it more the scope of the statistician in this sort of work to consider what causes may be excluded?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: The methods we used test hypotheses. Each of the three causes I proposed, we treated as a hypothesis. The methods allow us to reject hypotheses or to find that data are consistent with a hypothesis; however, the matters do not allow us to prove a hypothesis.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: With that overview of what you found yourself engaged in and the scope of the statistician's skill, range of his potential skill as applied in this case, can we now go back, please, to page 3. There are one or two things I wanted to clarify in the report, and it will be helpful to have those pages on the overhead projector so that people can follow what I'm asking about. And "Data and analysis," paragraph 1.2, you set out, as we already know, that you went to Morina, which is the one border point in the south-west of Kosovo, north of Albania.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Could one border point be sufficient? What's your comment on that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: This border point could be sufficient because, according to the available data, I believe that more than half of all Kosovar Albanians who left Kosovo did so through this point. In the report mentioned earlier that looks specifically at refugee flow, we found that all the other evidence available from other border points in Albania as well as the border points in Macedonia and data from Bosnia, Kosovars who went to Bosnia, suggest that their movement patterns and departure patterns were substantially similar to the patterns found among refugees who entered Albania. So, yes, I believe these data are sufficient for these conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The second bullet point of the same paragraph turns from the material you had in respect of refugee flow to the data you had in respect of killings, because as we're going to discover, you were looking at simultaneously -- not simultaneously. In the course of your work, you were looking both at refugee flow and at killings. Set out there and just run through for us the sources of information you had to tell you when, where, and whatever else you knew about killings.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: We learned about killings from interviews conducted by the American Bar Association, Central and East European Law Initiative, and their partners, interviews that they conducted, as well as interviews conducted by Human Rights Watch and interviews conducted by the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe. We --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So that - just pausing - are three, as it were, narrative records.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Right. And then you had a fourth record or fourth source.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes. And those were the exhumation records of the exhumations conducted by international teams on behalf of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So you did not have and therefore did not rely on witness statements of the ICTY, OTP?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You did have records in relation to the bodies found and material in relation to that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Human Rights Watch -- I beg your pardon. OSCE's records are, of course -- well, you better tell us if they are. Are those records that are also reflected in the two OSCE reports, one on the suffering of the Kosovar Albanians and one on the Serbs --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- the KLA?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And as we can see, in all, "The statistical analysis of killings aggregates information from more than 15.000 interviews and exhumation reports."

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right. Can we go now just to clarify one or two things on page 4. At the bottom of page, I think, "Statistical analysis of refugee flow." We've already looked at the graph because I wanted to provide the Court with an overview.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The top of that paragraph. Well -- thank you very much. That's -- no. Paragraph 3. Thank you. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You set out in this part of your report a description of the departure of ethnic Albanians from Kosovo from late March to May of 1999, saying that approximately 95 per cent of the Kosovo Albanian refugees who did so entered between the 24th of March and the 19th of May. And there's a reference. It says: "(Ball 2000, p.5)." Is that a reference to one of the two earlier reports published publicly that you've already spoken about?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was the work of those reports, although you yourself judged them not to be sufficient for presenting to Court in themselves, was the work of those earlier reports incorporated in the report that you have presented to this Court?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The 95 per cent, is that an estimate?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is it one by which you stand?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In what way? Just tell us about it.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: I used the border records supplemented by the UNHCR records and the much smaller head-count records done by the Albanian government's emergency management group in May, and I divided the refugees who flowed in during this period from those who flowed in either before or after, according to those records, and calculated a simple proportion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Footnote 6 we may focus on. I think deal -- it says at the end of it --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's it, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Says this: "The three phases..." and we've already looked at the diagram. We'll look at it once more in its first depiction. But it says this: "The three phases reflect patterns of refugees departing their homes, not the patterns of refugees crossing the border. On any given day, slightly more than half of the refugees who crossed the border had left their homes earlier that same day. However, the remaining refugees crossing the border that day had been in transit for longer times. The transit delay was accounted for in the analysis of the data." Well, you've already dealt with that in general. How did you calculate the transit delay for your statistical purposes?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: I had three surveys that had been conducted in refugee camps and other refugee housing locations in Albania and Macedonia during March through June of 1999. In those surveys, refugees reported the sequence of events that took them from their homes, their home departure, to the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. camps. From that, I was able to calculate the transit time for refugees and then look at that time for refugees who left different places and different times and compare the process of transit in a statistical sense over those different -- over refugees from different times -- different places and who had left at different times.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, if we go back to page 5 on which I have one supplementary question and following which, with the Chamber's leave, I would seek a one-minute private session to deal with the ordering of witnesses today and tomorrow, looking at page 5 again, and just to remind us, the graph at the top is the graph from the material that you had available on refugee flow, adjusted for the time that people left their homes before they reached the border; yes?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we can go down the page to the last paragraph, you say this in the last sentence: "The mass exodus of Kosovar Albanians on this scale and in this pattern could only have been driven by a common cause." We've seen three peaks. Common cause or two or three different causes? Can you help us?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: By "common cause" here, my co-authors and I refer to the -- that the refugees who departed would have had a cause common with respect to each other. At this point, we, without additional data, I don't think we could distinguish between whether there was one cause for all three peaks or three different causes. Additional data would allow us to refine that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Or I suppose, indeed, two causes and one cause, or two causes, rather.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Any combination, sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Turning to page 6, on which I have a few questions --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't know if that would be a convenient moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If there's another matter you want to raise, we'll adjourn now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Dr. Ball, you are giving evidence. Don't speak to anybody about it during the adjournment or any other adjournments there may be until it's over, and that does include members of the Prosecution team. Could you be back, please, at half past 2.00. Yes. We'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can Dr. Ball withdraw? It has nothing to do with him, I hasten to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.05 p.m. 24 25

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Page 6 of the report. We'll be looking at all of this. This has just been laid on the overhead projector, and I'd ask the booth to focus on relevant parts as we require them. This is one of about two or three parts of the report which need some explanation, for they are, to a degree, technical.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we look at the body of the report first, at the end of the first paragraph, we see a reference to 10.000 victims - thank you very much - reported by name. This process identified 4.400 unique individuals. In a couple of sentences, explain how 10.000 reduces to 4.400.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Many of the people who were reported to the data-gathering projects that I described earlier are reported by more than one witness, so a particular individual may be reported two or three times. One individual in particular, you'll remember, was reported 27 distinct times to one of the four projects. So we removed the individual - I mean the duplicate references - we identified them and removed them, and then we identified the references which were in common among more than one project. Someone may have been reported to the OSCE but also identified in an exhumation. After all of those reductions are complete, we are left with 4.400 unique individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's now go to the next paragraph, which begins in this way: "Second, because the victims identified in the data sources were not the only victims of killings, it was necessary to estimate the number of undocumented victims to determine the overall estimate of total number killed. This figure, 10.356 ..." I pause there straight away. Ten thousand, three hundred and fifty-six, the estimated number, is rather close to the 10.000 figure from which the reduced figure was itself derived. Is there significance in the similarity figures or is that entirely coincidental?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Entirely coincidental.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So you're now going from your 4.400 reduced figure to calculate another figure, and as you say in the paragraph, "generated by means of a widely used demographic statistical technique known as multiple systems estimation." In terms that the layperson can understand, please explain.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Multiple systems estimation uses the overlap among multiple projects to determine how many people fall outside the documentation of any of those projects. So, for example, there were 4.400 unique individuals reported by name to one or more of the four projects. There are some additional numbers of people who were not reported by name to any project. Our effort is to estimate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, because of the constraints of time and because this is a technical matter, I am probably going to leave it there, although I know there are illustrative diagrams you can draw to help us, and I may ask you to come back to one of them. But am I right in suggesting this: Because you had four sources of information - not just one, not just two, not just three, but four - differently prepared, you're able to engage in this multiple systems estimation to reach an approximate, an estimated global figure?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes. The method can be done with only two systems. With the addition of each additional system, we gain the ability to more deeply test our assumptions. Four systems is a quite thorough test.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, you, of course, proceeded in your report on the base of 10.356; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But it happens - and this is shown in the footnotes to this page - it happens that you had available to you, and we can see it at footnote 10, I think, some other independent studies that had been prepared in entirely different ways; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And so do these operate not as part of your database but as a check, if you like --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- something to cause you to look again if they are wildly different? In this case, if we look at the reports, PHR report of ABA/AAAS, what figure did that reach by a different system?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: The Physicians for Human Rights -- Human Rights report, cited as "PHR," approximated 9.600 deaths.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then if we go to the other one, which was Spiegel and Salama?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes. They are epidemiologists at the Centre for Disease Control.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What figure did they reach? Although I think they included a year that you didn't include.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: That's right. Their estimate includes 1998, which is excluded from our analysis. They reached a figure of approximately 12.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So more than you, but they've got another year.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Plus the months from January to mid-March, which are not in -- of 1999, which are not in our study.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So thus you reached your figure of 10.356. And if we then take that figure and look at the top of the page to the two graphs, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's all right. I think the booth will do it for us. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We now see at the top the same graph of "People leaving their homes" prepared in the way you've already described, but we now have underneath it a "People killed" graph. And is this prepared on the basis of raw material in the loose way I used or is this prepared on the basis of the figures as derived from multiple systems estimation?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: This is from multiple systems estimation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What do we notice about the similarity or dissimilarity of the shape of this graph in comparison with the earlier graph?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: They are very similar in several respects.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry again to the interpreters. I've not been leaving a gap.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My mistake, Dr. Ball. I will try and do so. Your observations about looking for a cause or separate causes for peaks, would that apply similarly for the "People killed" graph?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes, the same reasoning would apply.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Page 7 of the report, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Text first, for the booth, and then the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The text still relates to the graph you've been showing, and it makes one further explanation that we should have in mind. "When the estimated number of people killed is considered over time, using the same two-day intervals employed with the refugee flow data..." and so on. Now, I don't think I got you to deal with the two-day interval. Perhaps you could now.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: As I described earlier, the data from the Albanian border guards was transformed into data on people leaving their home by using the transit time. The transit time comes from surveys. As I described, several hundred surveys from my own project plus those from two other projects. When we look at the survey data day by day, there are some days with no data, and that's because we -- a survey is conducted with only a small sample. So on a day with relatively few refugees crossing the border, there are relatively few survey datum about it. As a result, there can be a lot of zeros if we look over time. Zeros may be real information or they may simply be points in the data that are insufficiently covered. By summing days together into two-day periods, we stabilise those estimates. I made this decision to do two-day intervals in the migration study, however, it proved useful throughout the subsequent study and the current study so we have maintained it all through for its property of giving us an additional stability, by which I mean specifically reducing the number of zero points in survey information.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Identifying intervals of whatever item or event material, is that a common and necessary technique in statistics?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Very much. The language that statisticians use is that of aggregating or adding things to bigger units, or disaggregating, breaking things into smaller units. It's a standard technique that every data analyst must employ to find the place where there's enough data to say something meaningful.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on to the next topic, which is first revealed by the map at the top of this page. Having prepared your first graph of "People killed," did you decide to break Kosovo down into four regions, north, east, south, and west, as shown on this map?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The divisions between parts of the territory have no relationship with political, geographical, or any other divisions. They're simply for statistical purposes.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: That's correct. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we go over now briefly to page 8. And at the top of the page we see "Refugee flow and killings by geographic location." "In addition to examining when refugee flow and killings happened, it is important to study where the events occurred. An analysis of the locations where the refugee flow originated, and the killings occurred, shows widespread patterns consistent with acts of violence associated with displacements." Those last few words are, I think, the conclusions of the following passage. Would that be correct? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we then go over -- we're going to come back to footnote 11, but can we now go to pages 9 and 10. On 9, Figure 4 at the top of the page has again the same "People leaving their homes" graph, but the bottom one now shows what?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: The bottom graph is the number of people killed. Both of the curves shown in Figure 4 are for people leaving their homes or people killed in the northern region.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. My mistake. The top map is not the familiar one. It's now unique to the northern region.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's been extracted. Thank you. And the bottom one, again prepared in the different way, still on the basis of the technique you told us about, is again just for the northern region.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: The bottom one is for the southern region.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry. The bottom of the two graphs at the top is for the -- at the top you've got two graphs, the top one being for "People leaving their homes" and the bottom of the two for "People killed" in the northern region. Do we here see similarity with early graphs or dissimilarity?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: The similarity we see in the two graphs of Figure 4 is with each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Here what's interesting to me in particular, I think, is the quite distinct peak in both graphs during phase 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The bottom figure is for the southern region. Again, it contains two graphs. Are they similar, one to the other, in statistics terms?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: These curves are quite similar to each other. They both show almost no activity in phase 2. Rather, in the southern region, nearly all the activity is concentrated in phase 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We see -- sorry. I'll just pause. We see on the "People leaving their homes" graph a little free-floating point with discussion in the text. I'll come back to that. If we go now to page 10 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, before you go to page 10, can I just ask the witness to return to the peaks in phase 2 of the northern region, and he highlighted the significance of those peaks. But the peak at the top, that is, for people leaving their homes, is actually higher than the peak at the bottom in respect of people killed. Is there -- does that indicate anything or ...?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The curves are not identical, as Your Honour has observed. What I think is most significant about these two curves is the existence of a very substantial peak during phase 2. That is what we will contrast with other regions in a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Reducing to non-technical terminology, correct me if I've got it wrong: Is it the fact and general quantum of a peak or trough that is significant rather than the precise scale of the peak? And if you don't accept that, don't adopt it simply because I've suggested it.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: The general pattern of high points and low points is important. The more closely they track each other, the more strongly a statistician would argue that they correlate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Right. We ought -- perhaps, since we're looking at figures 4 and 5, still on page 9, is it important for us just to have in mind that the scale -- the vertical scale in each graph is in fact different because you've adjusted the graphs to the maximum number of either people leaving their homes or people killed to make best use of the space?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: That's right. More than -- approximately 40 times more people left their homes and are represented in these graphs than were killed, so the scales must, by necessity, be different.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And indeed, as between the northern and southern region, the graph at the top, people-leaving graph is 7.900, the bottom people-leaving graph is 24.000?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And similar differences, even more substantial in proportionate terms, I think, as seen on page 10, which shows the eastern region at the top and the western region at the bottom. By now we can probably start to work things out for ourselves. In each case, the people-leaving and people-killed graphs, do they have similarities to each other?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: However, is the western region graph similar or dissimilar from the eastern?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: The west is dissimilar from the east.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Coming back to page 9, does it have any points of similarity with the southern?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes. The western and southern patterns are quite similar, as distinguished by absence of significant peak during phase 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Going back from page 9, and in particular, we'll go back to page 8, because I drew your attention to the free-standing point that is said to require discussion in the text. On the footnote at page 8, do you observe that there is an anomalous point in the southern region in late May? It's at the footnote on that page, right down at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes, we do observe that, my co-authors and I.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you say this in the text of the footnote: "This estimate of more than 200 people killed in one two-day period results from fewer than 20 documented killings." And then you say this: "Appropriately, this point also has a high level of error associated with it, as shown in Appendix 2, Figure 12. As is clear in that figure, most points have modest errors which do not weaken the interpretation of the pattern. This point, however, has a sufficiently wide margin of error that the point may not be significantly different from zero." Two or three things from that: If statisticians, or even Their Honours, want to follow the error or the margin of error calculations, they may do so at Appendix 2. I think it's page 53. We don't need to turn to it. But looking at any one of the graphs - page 9 is open before me - do the figures represented on these graphs have margins of error associated with them?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes. Every point in the people-killed graphs has a margin of error.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you assess those margins of error to ensure that they are not at such a level as to invalidate the figure that you're representing?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes, we do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The free-standing point dealt with in the footnote and to be seen on Figure 5 is one which you eliminate because of the scale of the error, the margin of error, but as to the other figures, have you allowed for the possibilities of margins of error, nevertheless standing by the graph that you've drawn?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes, we have.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. In that case, may we turn to page 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just one minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure. You might have mentioned this, but regarding the date in the refugee flow data, do they refer to the date when the refugees entered the border or those when they left their villages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We refer to the latter, the dates they left their villages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Page 11. We start with a text, which actually begins on the previous page, 8. Don't worry about that. The text explains how you're exploring the hypotheses you've already described; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So we can see at the beginning of the text: "However, if airstrikes and KLA activity do not precede the peaks in the number of killings ... then the causal relationship should be ... rejected." Well, let's just have from you your approach to connection or non-connection of either KLA activity or, in due course, NATO activity, with refugee movement or killings. What was your approach?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Our idea is that if something is to cause something else, then the cause must precede the effect. Accordingly, we looked at the peak level of killings and refugee flow for each municipality. There are 29. We then considered whether, during the two-day period of the peak or in the preceding two-day period, there was some KLA activity. If we found any KLA activity whatsoever in the period of the peak or in the period immediately preceding the peak, we counted that in the first row. However, if we found KLA activity either not at all in that municipality or following the peak, we counted it in the second row. Finally, if KLA activity preceded the peak of the killings or refugee flow by more than four days, we counted that as an inconclusive pattern.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Right. Well, before we look at the table that sets out your findings, it's necessary to know, first for the KLA and then for NATO, what your sources of material were on the basis of which you then built the table. Let's deal with KLA first. What sources of material for KLA activity did you have and rely on?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: We began, my co-authors and I, began by examining open sources that were placed on Internet by the government of Yugoslavia, and as well as Serbian non-governmental organisations. These documented casualties suffered by Serb authorities in Kosovo as a result of KLA attacks, and the sources documented exchanges of fire, battles, between KLA forces and Yugoslav government or police forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was that your only source or did you have other sources for KLA?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: We supplemented those sources with additional sources provided to us by the Office of the Prosecutor. The open sources in total constituted 55 per cent of our source material, and the Tribunal sources constituted 45 per cent of our sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Going back, as I said I would when His Honour Judge Robinson asked you this morning, to the topic of your instructions by the Office of the Prosecutor, two things about the material - three things - about the material provided by the Office of the Prosecutor: One, was it statements or was it reduced to a statistical or summarised form?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: It was reduced to a highly summarised form.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Second, how did that material compare in its general shape and effect with the 55 per cent of open-source material that you had obtained from Serb sources?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: In the statistical terms, they looked approximately the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Third, at the time that that material was provided to you, had the Office of the Prosecutor any advance knowledge or knowledge of the findings to which your report may have been moving?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: When I met with the Office of the Prosecutor's representatives in early November, we had none of the results on killing that are presented here complete. However, the migration report had been in the public domain for a year and a half or so, so that was available to anyone who wanted to look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Back to the text: In the next paragraph, beginning "To test the conclusions drawn by this method, we used another statistical method to consider the joint correlations of ..." I'll come back to that perhaps later. But -- yes, I'll come back to that later. Let's go to the chart at the top of the page, then, please, if we can. Reminding ourselves that "preceded or coincided with peak" means really the four-day period that ends in the peak; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of the 29 municipalities, there was killing preceded by KLA activity in 11; killing followed by KLA activity in 12; and killing with inconclusive findings as to KLA activity - either none or outside those parameters - in 6.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the refugee flow shows respectively 10 for Preceded or coincided, 11 for Followed, and 8 for Inconclusive. The percentages in each case being set out. What does that tell you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: If we hypothesise that KLA activity directly or indirectly caused killing or refugee flow, we would expect that KLA attacks and activity would be very frequently present at the peak of the hypothesised cause. I believe that this table shows that there is no KLA activity at all preceding the peak in more municipalities than we see the hypothesised coincidence. We interpret this to mean that this tends to reject the hypothesis that the KLA was the cause of killings and refugee flow.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May we now move to the possible significance of NATO, page 12. What were your sources of information for NATO attacks on a geographical basis so as to explain or not to explain killings and refugee flow?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: The data on NATO airstrikes came exclusively from Yugoslav press and government sources that were publicly available in the period approximately June to August 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You restricted yourself to that source for what reason?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: There were two reasons: One, because my two phone calls to the US Department of Defence went unanswered and unreturned, so I did not get data from the US side; but second, it seemed to me the best possible test of this hypothesis to use the data from Yugoslavia. At the time, the hypothesis I was focusing on was the relationship between NATO airstrikes and refugee flow. So the claim that NATO airstrikes had motivated in some way refugee flow was in part advanced by authorities in the Yugoslav government. It seemed to me the best test of that hypothesis to use data from Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The table at the top of page 11, in a form similar to the previous table, shows thus that there were NATO airstrikes preceding refugee flow in three of the 29 municipalities. There were -- did I say that correctly?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: I think it's preceding in killings in three.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In killings, I should have said, in three of the municipalities. There were airstrikes preceding refugee flow in nine of the municipalities. The remaining figures, 20 and 6, 13 and 7 being municipalities where there was either such strikes or inconclusive Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. material. Sorry, such strikes following or inconclusive material.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, what does that tell you about the possible significance of NATO airstrikes in the killings or the refugee flow?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
