utterances.text: The pattern that in 20 municipalities NATO airstrikes followed the -- the first NATO airstrike followed the peak of killings makes NATO airstrikes a highly implausible cause of the pattern of killings. After all, the peak occurred and passed before the first airstrike in 20 municipalities. Similarly for refugee flow, NATO airstrikes are an implausible motivator, directly or indirectly, for refugee flow since, in 13 municipalities, the peak came and went without the first airstrike having occurred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Excuse me once again. Whether the NATO bombing preceded or not was decided municipality by municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So if a nearby village was bombed yesterday and the villagers left on today and it was bombed tomorrow, so that was -- you mean that it is not -- the NATO bombing was not preceded in that case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the nearby village was across a municipal border --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- that would be correct. We consider that in the next section.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we come back briefly to page 11, because I said there was something that needed explanation, it being a term of art, that we should have explained on the record for those of us who will be reading the report in months to come. In the middle of the page you set out this: "To test the conclusions drawn by this method, we used another statistical method..." Are we now moving to a different tool from the one we've already looked at?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "... to consider the joint correlations of KLA and NATO activity with refugee flow and killing patterns. The point is to use the second statistical technique..." and then these words, "... to control for the correlation of KLA activity...." We're going to see the word, or we may see the words "control for" elsewhere in your report. It's a term of art. What does it mean?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: In this analysis, we are examining first the pattern of killings over time and space and then the pattern of refugee flow over time and space. Our question is: What statistical relationship do the patterns of NATO airstrike and KLA activity have with the patterns of killing and refugee flow? The technique employed is to use the statistical relationship of KLA activity and NATO airstrikes to make an estimate of each point and then remove the effect of that estimate from the pattern, from the pattern of killing or migration. That removal is what we mean by "control for."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we leave this page, and I should have dealt with this earlier, but I'd just like you to explain footnote 12, which actually relates to the earlier -- the earlier examination reflected in the two tables, the KLA and the NATO tables. You say that, "... for this analysis, we used only the number of reported killings, not the estimated total number." Just explain that, please.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: In order to determine when the peak occurred for killings in Figure 8 and 9, we took the simple number of victims reported in each municipality over time. That is, we used only the 4.400 people whose names we can list in order to conduct the analysis in figures 8 and 9. The reason was that, as I discussed earlier in my description of the two-day periods, when we break the data down to 29 municipalities, it is too thin. There is not enough data. There are too many zeros to make the estimates.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. And I remind the -- it may help if we just remind the learned Judges that your initial process was to go from the figure of 10.000-odd or down to 4.400 and then to expand it, in the method you've described, to 10.356. What you're saying is, on this occasion, you couldn't do that second step?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In general -- and I'm sorry to have done this slightly out of order, but there it is. In general, how conservative were the figures you were relying on in every stage of your report?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: We made every attempt to be as conservative as possible. In this sense, I mean conservative as we made decisions that would all tend to reduce the total estimate and to reduce the estimates at each space-and-time point. The point of that was to present a statistical case which would be as favourable as possible to the hypotheses which we ultimately have rejected here, but we gave that the strongest test we could. The most obvious sense of conservatism that I can give as an example is that whenever we compared two people who may potentially -- two names which potentially might refer to the same person, we assumed that the names did refer to the same person unless we were able to demonstrate positively that they did not refer to the same person. Again, that tends to reduce the total lists and to reduce the overall estimates.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: After that digression, then I can return to the second method, the controlling-for method. Can we go to page 13 of a 15, 16-page report? We're approaching its conclusion. Here is the third and, I think, last part of the report where we'll have to have some guidance on statistical concepts from you. If we look at the graph at the top of the page, we can see a new word featuring, underneath "People killed" and another line, called "Residuals." People can consume technical ideas in different ways, sometimes by reference to the matter in hand, sometimes by reference to generalities. Can you give us, in a sentence or so, first of all, how Residuals operates in the most general terms? And then we'll look at the facts of this case.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Referring to the discussion of controlling for, if we think about the top line in Figure 10, the dark line which --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You're now dealing with specifically on the facts of this case. I was wondering if you could just help us conceptually with what a residual is --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- and then we'll come to the facts of the case.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: When we wish to examine the effect of one variable upon another, we control for, as I discussed, the hypothesised cause and then we can look at the resulting pattern in the hypothesised effect. If we deduct that quantity created or accounted for by the cause, the remaining value from the original is called the residual, that which remains. The pattern of the residual can tell us a great deal about the structure of the explanation, the internal relationship of these two variables.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now let's, having described it in conceptual terms, look at Figure 10, the facts of this case. What do these two lines, "People killed" and "Residuals" show?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: The bottom line, the Residuals, describes the net effect or that which remains after we have controlled for KLA activity and NATO airstrikes. What is striking about the residual pattern is that it largely follows the original pattern. They follow quite closely.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll come to the significance of that in a minute, because I think it may help the learned Judges if we break it down step-by-step. The top line is the line we've already seen before, for example, on page 6.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What you're doing in reaching the residual is deducting in some statistical way that part of that line which is explained by NATO and KLA activity; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: That is -- that's broadly correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were it the case that NATO/KLA activity explained every killing, what would be left? What would be the Residual line?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: The Residual line, if the explanation were stronger, the Residual line would be merely a roughly flat line, squiggling around the horizontal axis.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Because you will have explained by the hypothesis everything on the Residual line?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: A statistical correlation would explain the original pattern, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So here you remove what may be explained by KLA or NATO activity and you're left with a line of shape similar to the original line.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What does that tell you as a statistician?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: It tells us that the explanation has not changed the pattern very much. The explanation provided by the statistical relationships of NATO airstrike activity and KLA activity does not explain the pattern of killing over time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Page 14, please. This figure, the figure at the top of the page, Figure 11, is the same exercise conducted for refugee flow; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Same thing: If it was wholly explained by KLA and NATO, it would be a flat line hovering around -- or a flat-ish line hovering around the north?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What do you say about the shape that we see of the Residual line?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: The Residual line does track the original pattern, with peaks and troughs at roughly the same points.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As strong as in the killings or not?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Less strong. Less strong.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We see here in footnote 17 that you suggest in the middle of the page in the text that it has -- let's just read that. Shall we go down in the text a little bit? The results, you say, are shown --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If the booth could take us down in the text a bit. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You say, in Figure 10 -- you set that out: "The same analysis can be performed for the refugee flow. The results are shown in Figure 11. As with killings, the pattern of the refugee flow, controlling for the correlations with the NATO and KLA patterns, is strongly similar to the original pattern. However, the statistical measures suggest that the KLA activity (but not NATO airstrikes) has a weak but noticeable relationship with the refugee flow pattern." Just explain that again.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: I think -- well, when a statistician looks at Figure 11, he or she will ask: There does seem to be some explanation here. Which factors might be responsible for that explanation? So she or he would want to conduct a more detailed analysis, looking at the individual factors - KLA activity and NATO activity - and consider their individual contributions to the explanation. We also, my co-authors and I, also felt that this warranted a more detailed analysis over both region and time, which we conducted, and that is referred to in the footnote.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And we should have in mind, without referring back to it, that the figures of refugee migration had shown different patterns regionally; in particular, the southern and the western differing from the northern and the east?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So if we can go, quite briefly, in the annexes of the report, to pages 59, 60, and 61. We can look at 59 very briefly.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: I believe you mean 58.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Oh, yes, 58 as well maybe. Yes, 58. 58, I think, requires some technical explanation. Can you give us that, please. What is it, first of all? It's headed "Regression Coefficients" and "Response Variables," and then we have a number of titles: "Killings Over Time and Region," and so on. Can you explain it, please.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: These are the coefficients, the actual statistical coefficients that are the model used for the residual analysis we just discussed. Each of the coefficients describes the relationship, all else being equal, between a particular variable and the response variable, that which we are trying to explain. So, for example, going to the top of the third column in the "KLA (kill)" variable under "Refugee Flow Over Time," the interpretation of the number -634.9 is that, all else being equal, in a given region, at a certain point in time, the presence of each additional Serb casualty caused by the KLA would result in 635 fewer refugees leaving that municipality - or excuse me, excuse me - that region in that time, in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. We're going to be able to understand this chart ourselves probably with but one more or, at the most, two more examples, but it's got one deficiency in it at the moment, by typographical error, and that is that there should be one more asterisk - we'll explain the asterisk - and the remaining asterisk should be in the figure immediately below that, 2.728.6; should it not?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: That's correct. There should be an asterisk there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the asterisks on page 58 - and it's either a single asterisk, as that last entry, or a double or a triple asterisk - what do they represent, or what do they signify, rather?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: The asterisks describe the relationship between the coefficient listed in the table and the error associated with that coefficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There can be cases where the error swamps the statistic so the statistic becomes of no value?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: That is correct. In fact, those statistics without asterisks should not be interpreted. They are -- the error is too great.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And in the most approximate terms, where the correcting error figure, in brackets, is half or more than the numeric figure above it, plus or minus, then the figure is of no value?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: It's quite close to half. It's actually -- but it's 1.96. But yes, in terms, you're correct. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The smaller the error figure is, as a proportion of the numeric figure above it, the larger the number of stars, the stronger the value of the conclusion?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Broadly, yes. Broadly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So let us then do one more example to see if we understand this. And "KLA (kill)," "KLA (battle)," self-explanatory, as is "NATO," but what about "Lag-KLA (battle)"? Can you explain that as a title for us?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes. "Lag" is the statistician's term for what happened in the previous period. So "Lag-KLA (battle)" is the effect of a battle that occurred in the previous two-day period to the migration or killing we are explaining. So we want to consider in this model not only what has happened in the current two-day period, but also what happened in the previous two-day period in order to explain the pattern of killings and refugee flow.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And so to check that we understand how the table may be read by the Chamber, or indeed by other statisticians who may look at the document, if we stay with "Lag-KLA (battle)" and then, at the top, "Killings Over Time and Region," so it's the figure 11.6, with 11.9 in brackets -- well, that won't do, because it hasn't got an asterisk to go against it, so we won't rely on that. "Lag-KLA (battle)" and then "Refugee Flow Over Time and Region," 2.138.4, with three asterisks, that interprets as --?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: All else being equal, and here I mean all the KLA killings and battles, NATO activity being equal, the effect of each additional KLA battle in a region is to predict 2.138.4 more refugees departing their homes on the next two-day period, in the following two-day period. So it's in the next two-day period.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you're referring to a battle, you're referring to a battle between the KLA and --?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: And Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Page 59, please, briefly. Simply, the charts at the top within the appendix, this is the same scheme of killings charted, with the residuals underneath, but now broken down by region. And taking it very shortly, do we see a close correlation of residuals and original chart in both north, east, south, and west?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes. The relationship is close in all four regions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The same conclusion; namely, that KLA or NATO activity does nothing to explain the pattern of killings.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Not quite nothing, but it does very little.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very little. Thank you. Page 60, please. When we look at refugee flow with the same approach, broken down by regions north, east, south, and west, to the eye, the residuals track less closely than with killings, although they track in the south and west, it may be, more closely than the north and east. But what would your interpretation be?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Following that, in the north and east, until the phase 2 peak in mid-April of refugee flow in both regions, the patterns, residual pattern, does not track very closely the original pattern. Then in that mid-April peak, they converge closely, then follow each other roughly through the end, with some divergences, some divergences in the less significant periods toward the end when the magnitudes are very small. In the south and west, the residual pattern actually tracks quite closely in the south, and closely, but not as closely, in the west, where there are a few smaller divergences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Judge Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Dr. Ball, I wanted to have clarified a few matters. In answer to me earlier, you said that when you first presented, I think, your first two reports to the OTP, you indicated that you would have to make them more rigorous for presentation in Court. I'd like you to tell me what you did to make it more rigorous. I heard you mention one particular matter which perhaps could have had that result; that is, you said wherever there was a conflict, then you took the course which was favourable to the hypothesis that you eventually rejected. If that is one, then you can say so and tell me what are the other methods that you used to make the presentation more rigorous.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is indeed one, the one that Your Honour listed. Let me highlight three others quite briefly. The first is that, relative to the first two reports, we sought, my co-authors and I sought much more extensive peer review, as we described at the beginning of the presentation, with a substantial committee of statisticians from Europe and the United States, each of whom had the opportunity to review two preliminary drafts of the report. In earlier work, I had been less formal and worked with a number of advisors who read drafts and made comments to me, but not in this much more formal process that we instituted for this report. The second additional rigour that we applied has to do with the matching process. Recall that the data source for killings are lists of names of people who have been described as having been killed in witness reports, and to do the estimation that we describe here, from 4.400, we have to determine which killings are in multiple reports. I have to look at the list from Human Rights Watch, several hundred names, and determine which of those names are also in the other lists. This is hard because there are a number of factors which complicate making exact comparisons. To assure that that was as reliable and rigorous a process as we could, every intersystem comparison, as I just described, between the ABA/CEELI data, the exhumation information data, the HRW data - Human Rights Watch data - and the OSCE data, every one of those comparisons was done by two or more different coders, different staff people, independently. So I -- every single one of those matches was done by two people, and many of them were done by three, some by four, and some by five. Those people went through an extensive training process, as described in Appendix 1. For purposes of your question, I think the most important note was that we were able to measure, and thus quantify, the reliability of the matching process, reliability here in a formal, statistical sense, which is that if we did it again, we would reach the same conclusions. That's what I mean by "reliability." The agreement between the raters was 94 per cent. Ninety-four per cent of the decisions were reached the same way by all the coders, all the staff people who looked at the names to make decisions about whether they should be matched. All the disagreements that were found in the remaining 6 per cent were reviewed by a supervisor and a final decision reached. So that's the second of the additional kinds of rigour we brought to this process that I had not done in earlier projects. It's very difficult. There's one more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The final one is that the statistical calculations that we've just been discussing, the estimation procedure and all this analysis, was done twice by two different people independently, on different computers, using different software, in fact, using completely different operating systems. We started with the same data, we established the mathematical procedure we were going to use, and then she, one of the co-authors here, and I independently wrote all of the software to do the estimation. And we kept doing it until our answers agreed to many different -- to many digits. We made sure that completely different estimation procedures, completely different software, different computers, different analysts, reached the same conclusions. Again, that's -- they're expensive, but we felt that it was warranted in this case, given the gravity of the questions. So those are the three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Notwithstanding the initial rigour and the additional rigour that you applied, are you able to put your conclusions any higher than what you said in relation to Figure 8 on page 11, that it tends to reject a particular hypothesis? Are you able to put it any higher than that, or that's the highest that you can put it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I can put it higher than that. And I think what I would say is at the point of Figure 8, the strongest conclusion, if I were to stop there, the strongest conclusion I would want to make is that it tends to reject. As we continue through these additional analyses which I've just described, we can make substantially stronger conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see. Okay. The next question I wanted to ask you was whether this statistical method that you have developed, whether it has been used in court proceedings before, in judicial proceedings.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me separate my answer into three small parts, if I may. The procedure used to describe the migration process is composed of a statistical tool kit of many different methods, each one of which would be easily recognisable to any professional statistician or demographer. I don't know if it is -- if those methods have been combined in this way before, but certainly the component methods would be widely used in any statistical presentation, including those that would be given before judicial proceedings. I do not have specific knowledge. On the second method, which is the multiple systems estimation, which uses the -- which estimates the total number of people killed, again I don't have specific knowledge about judicial use; however, this method is widely used to adjust censuses, which, as Your Honours are probably aware, is the basis for legislative apportionment, and so tends to have very high stakes. So it is a closely investigated scientific method. It is well known. And since censuses are always partial - they never count everybody - this is the method to which demographers turn to to adjust censuses. In the third answer, I can answer yes, although I can't provide examples. In the regression analysis, in the residual analysis, this is among the most common statistical techniques used anywhere. I mean, any time social scientists, statisticians, or demographers want to examine the relationship of several or many variables over a large --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm talking about court proceedings in particular.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe it must have been, sir, Your Honour. I don't know of a specific case. I'm not a lawyer, so I'm unfamiliar with the details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The next matter that you can help me with is this: I can understand the utility of your method in analysing broad patterns and broad trends, but in this case, we are concerned with specific allegations that relate to particular geographical areas. There's an allegation that there was a movement of people from A to B. This was caused by a particular phenomenon. There is evidence that, prior to the movement, there was KLA activity, there was NATO activity, and there was Serb activity. The task which the Trial Chamber has is to determine what was the cause in relation to the particular charges in the indictment. I'm not sure I understand how your statistical method, which I think is very useful for broad patterns of conduct, is particularly helpful in relation to that specific issue which is particular and specific to a particular area and in relation to which there may or may not be evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that when I reach the conclusions of the -- my direct presentation, it may shed some light on your question about the causes which you've proposed and which I've adopted as hypotheses here, as I will find two of those causes to be statistically implausible, given the available evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Where, for example, the NATO bombing took place after the movement. I mean, I would have thought the conclusion that the NATO bombing was not the cause to be quite an unremarkable conclusion. But the real issue is where we have evidence of the two or three phenomena I mentioned taking place before and where there is a conflict, and that is what I think we need help with, and I'm trying to see how your exercise helps us with that particular issue. But I understand you'll be coming to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We have yet to reach the conclusions, but in light of the questions you've been asked, just a couple of matters to pick up on. First of all, just dealing with peer review. Can we find some examples in the report? I think one may be at page 61 of additional things that you did as a result of peer review suggestion. Am I right about page 61?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I wasn't proposing to go into it in detail for the reason you'll give in a second, but "Estimated killings over time with alternative date assignments," what do these mean, "alternative date assignments"?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Much of our argument turns on whether killings in this case happened exactly at the time that we estimate that they occurred, and so a reasonable question might be: What if the witnesses got the dates wrong? What would happen to your analysis? So our response to that quite reasonable question is to look at each date reported by the witnesses and move them as far earlier and later as is remotely plausible. And I can describe how that was done in detail if there are additional questions. But we shifted the dates as early and as late as were possible or we thought were plausible for each date.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This was a peer review proposal?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: It was a question that was asked, simply: What would happen to your analysis if the date reporting were imprecise?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And -- sorry. I mustn't go too fast. And the charts or graphs we see, did they lead to any different conclusion of any kind?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: I do not think so. I believe they are substantially the same, given the radical adjustment that we made to test that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The second point arising from His Honour's questions, or one of them, in particular multiple systems estimation and its use in court, in fact, multiple systems estimation was not used for the first and, in a sense, most readily accessible conclusions in figures 8 and 9, was it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It was used in the others.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: It was used in the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But now let's come to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before you do, it's now five to four. Plainly we're Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. not going to get to another witness tonight. Four o'clock is the time for a break. Are you going to be finished shortly?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I would think I'll be finished shortly because I only have the conclusion page of the witness to go to apart from one or two other references.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a comment to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Milosevic, make it shortly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] An objection, in fact. Very briefly. As you're speaking about the next witness, I did not ask for any postponement of the cross-examination. I have heard that that was something that one of the friends of the Court asked for. But as you know, the friends of Court do not represent me. And a moment ago when I showed a whole lot of papers, I did so, I showed them as being an example of the improper manner and prejudicial manner and not as being my request for anything, for any kind of understanding, because there's no understanding for me at all, and especially no understanding with respect to my possible consultations with the advisors and consultants that the other side mentioned, because I cannot contact my advisors other than by telephone. So please bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us see what you're saying. Are you saying you want to cross-examine the witness now?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that I did not ask for any postponement of cross-examination, which implies that I shall continue, once this witness finishes his testimony, with my right to examine him in cross-examination. That is, I suppose, something which is the normal order of the day and nothing that I make a special request of or for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll adjourn now for five minutes for a break and then we'll go on with the rest of the evidence. --- Break taken at 3.55 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we can now go to the conclusions on page 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, just to explain, the questions that I asked, I had intended to ask them after your examination-in-chief. So I thought you had finished, because it's not my style to interrupt examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm grateful for your explaining that. No, no. I diverted to the appendices because they were referred to in the body of the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Page 15, then, please. The format of it, we can see you've already been dealing with the two hypotheses. First of all, KLA, NATO, and then with the Yugoslav forces, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A little up the page, please, if we may. The other way. Thank you very much. A bit further. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Dr. Ball, first of all, on the analysis so far described using the different techniques and samplings that you've referred to, what was your conclusion as to the possible involvement of NATO and or the KLA in either the refugee movement or the killings?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: First, we rejected the hypothesis that NATO involvement caused either killing or the migration. In both of the methods, NATO showed inadequate correlations to be considered a plausible cause. Therefore, we rejected the hypothesis that NATO was a cause of either killing or migration patterns. Second, we reject the hypothesis that KLA activity caused the patterns, the statistical patterns, of killing. Thus KLA activity is not a plausible cause for more than a small fraction of the killing, a cause directly or indirectly of more than a small fraction of the killings. The fourth sub-piece of it is a bit more complex, as we were discussing earlier. There does seem to be some correlation at certain times and certain regions between KLA activity and refugee flow.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And by "KLA activity," as you've already told me, you were referring to KLA/Serb conflict?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: That's right. Serb casualties caused by the KLA and exchanges of fire between KLA forces and Yugoslav forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's now turn to the third hypothesis which we can see on the page, headed "Yugoslav forces."

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Turning to that third hypothesis, you say in your report that: "Yugoslav forces organised and implemented a systematic campaign of violence resulting in killings and refugee flow: the statistical analysis of correlations cannot prove that the Yugoslav forces were the external influence responsible for the observed patterns. However, the findings of this study are consistent with the hypothesis that action by Yugoslav forces was the cause of the killings and refugee flow." Just pausing there and knowing that there's something in the following paragraph, does that remain your opinion?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And of course, as well as -- I mustn't go too fast, particularly at this time of the day. As well as peaks, there are troughs in both the refugee flow and in the killings, and do you find one circumstantial link that may assist?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Which would be the best chart for us to look at to see this circumstantial link, or will any of them do?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Any of them will do. Perhaps Figure 2 is the clearest. I believe from page -- it might be 6. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I wonder if you can just lay that back on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Page 6, the earliest and, in one way, the simplest, but the others to similar effect. Yes, please go on.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: On the evening of April 6th, Yugoslav official sources announced a unilateral ceasefire by Yugoslav forces to honour Orthodox Easter, which that year fell on April 11th, Sunday. The 6th of April was a Tuesday, and the announcement was made that evening. On the following day, what is very interesting is that using these widely differing statistical techniques and completely different data, we find a consistent and drastic decline in both refugee movement and people being killed. That decline is exactly coincidental in time with the Yugoslav government declaration of a ceasefire. Both people leaving their homes and people killed declined drastically on the 7th and remained at low levels for several days. I don't know if the Yugoslav government rescinded the ceasefire, but it seems that it -- that hostilities began again sometime during the weekend, approximately at the time of Orthodox Easter. Both people leaving their homes and people killed increase again at that point. That circumstantial link, which is, I think, quite dramatic in light of the very high levels of killing and refugee flow a few days prior to the ceasefire announcement, leads my co-authors and I to confirm - or, excuse me - to state that the evidence that we have found, the statistical evidence, is consistent with the hypothesis that Yugoslav forces are the cause of the observed patterns.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. In addition to requests from your peer review to consider certain matters and to add matters to your report, did you receive a request or instructions from the Office of the Prosecutor, to which you responded by the short two-and-a-half, three-page supplement, with annexes, that's been served on the Court?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes. We were -- several requests were made of us in February this year.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to break them down, now that we are familiar with what you were doing, to very simple proposition and very simple conclusions, you being in a position to turn any questioner to the workings it asked. Were you asked to do some further breakdowns and to check results by different broken-down approaches?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes, we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Explain just in a sentence or so.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: We were asked to consider the relationship between refugee flow and killing directly, those two compared to each other, using the same method that we looked at in Figures 8 and 9, with the different percentages. We called that the peaks-versus-presence method.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: We conducted the analysis, and the hypothesis there would be that if the two series are closely related, then we would find the presence of killings before the peak refugee flow for each municipality, there would be a high level of coincidence there. Similarly, we would expect that the peak in killings would coincide with or occur just before a very high - or, excuse me - a recorded refugee flow. We found that in both cases, the number of municipalities which satisfy the hypothesis was quite high, 69 and 83 per cent respectively.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The second exercise you were asked to perform?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: We were also to consider the independent effects of the NATO and KLA activity on killing and migration.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So if we want to look at a chart or a map and say that you reconsidered the same topic but now with one factor on its own, which would be the best ones to look at? Figures 10 and 11 in the original?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Figures 10 and 11 would be the ones we took apart in the subsequent figures.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So Figures 10 and 11 deal with KLA and NATO collectively. You then dealt with them separately?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are the conclusions the same or different?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: The conclusions are the same, that bombing has very little effect on either pattern -- NATO airstrikes, bombing, has very little effect on either pattern. KLA activity has no effect on killing but seems to have a relationship with refugee flow in the northern and eastern regions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And my last question, which is just a matter of detail, but it may help the Chamber. If you can just look at Appendix 3, the additional sources on KLA and NATO activity, please. It's page -- just the page before page 64. It's an unnumbered page, so it's really 63, but it hasn't got a number on it. Two pages of this, I think, that page and the following page. To give us an idea of the rigour of your report, this is simply your sources or additional sources, as you explain, for KLA and NATO activity. You list, starting with the Albanian Human Rights Group and running on that page down to Kosovapress, and on the following page you can see all the names and bodies to which you referred. On the following page, we pick it up at Kosovar Media and run down to V.I.P. Daily News Report. Are these all bodies that you turned to or scoured or searched for details of NATO and KLA activity in order to run your hypothesis?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes. The NATO activity was limited to the Yugoslav sources, a subset of the ones listed here, but all of these contributed elements to the sources we used for the KLA measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Ball. If you wait there, you may be asked some further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish, first and foremost, to finish with my objection, because you interrupted me. I consider this to be an elementary minimum of decency --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the objection?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said why and for what reason I illustrated the extreme incorrectness and isolation and every possible way of depriving me of any equality before this illegal institution of yours. I asked for a minimum of decency at least for this list of witnesses that the opposing party is bringing here, that I should be given this list at least a week in advance, and I expect to be given in the future a list of the right order of witnesses one week in advance. As for this witness, I shall start with the cross-examination immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order to put the first question I have, I shall first quote what it says in these papers, because there is an explanation here of the organisation that the witness works for, that is to say, the American Association for the Advancement of Science, et cetera. This is what it says here: [As interpreted] "The material contained here are the opinions of the author and editors and cannot be considered to be the view of the American Association for the Advancement of Science...," in parentheses, "... (The original American Association for the Advancement of Science, AAAS)...." And further on, "... or the Central and East European Law Initiative." So they cannot be construed to be the view of either one institution or the other. And also, it says here: "The ABA/CEELI, the American Bar Association, Central and East European Law Initiative, or any of the contributing organisations. The AAAS Committee on Scientific Freedom and Responsibility ... in accordance with its mandated and Association policy, supports publication of this report as a scientific contribution to human rights. The interpretations and conclusions are those of the authors and do not purport to represent the views of the AAAS Board, Council, the CSFR, or the members of the Association." So they do not represent the views of any one of them. "Likewise, the views expressed herein have not been approved by the House of Delegates or the Board of Governors of the ABA and, accordingly should not be construed as representing the policy of the ABA. "Nothing contained in this publication is to be considered as the rendering of legal advice for specific cases, and readers are responsible for obtaining such advice from their own legal counsel. This publication and any forms and agreements herein are intended for educational and informational purposes only." That's what it says here. Signed by the American Association for the Advancement of Science. Since this is what it says here, my first question is the following: What it says here, does that mean that your work cannot be used for purposes of the indictment?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: This report is not legal advice. I am not a lawyer. I am, however, a scientist, and I believe that I can offer some scientific insight into these patterns. That has been my effort.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You have said that this is statistical research.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, is there a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is a question. This is statistical research.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this is not sociological research.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Something may be simultaneously sociological and statistical. "Statistical" refers to the methodological approach taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You spoke exclusively about statistics and statistics experts. There are no elements of sociological research in here. Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: The question confuses me. I think that sociological research in my country and as practised at the university where I took my doctorate is highly quantitative in nature and this would be recognised, I believe, by any American or probably most European sociologists as sociology. "Statistical," as I said earlier, refers to the methods that were used.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: These are not methods; these are methodological procedures that you apply. There is a major difference between a method and methodological approach. Do you know how to explain the difference between a method, a sociological method, for example, and a methodological procedure that you applied here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the point of this question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, what is the point of explaining that this statistical analysis of incorrect data is a sociological research? The witness mentioned the application of a method. He mentioned that all sociologists accept, espouse, quantitative methods. Quantitative methods have their limited reaches, and not everything can be explained by quantitative methods, because if everything could be explained statistically, then there would be no need for sociology to exist, as the most general of sciences about society. Therefore, I ask the witness, who, as we have heard, has a doctorate in sociology, to define briefly the difference between sociological method and methodological procedure applied herein.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is an irrelevant question. Ask him about his evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, you cannot restrict me in my questions, especially --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I can in what is relevant. Perhaps Dr. Ball can help us. You've heard what's being put. Is there any point that you think you can answer in relation to it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That answer is sufficient for me as well. As a doctor of sociology, you cannot answer this question about the difference --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I'm not going to make any comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So in addition to the fact that we have such an explanation of the American association, your answer to the question whether this explanation precludes the possibility of using your work for the needs and purposes of the indictment is that you are not a lawyer. You didn't say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: I'm not a lawyer, and therefore I do not believe I'm competent to speak to whether this is -- this answers your question or not. That's my answer. I'm a statistician. I've offered statistical and sociological analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's precisely what I have been asserting, that you are a statistician, and that this is not a sociological analysis but a statistical approach. My next question: Were you asked to look at the movements of Serb refugees during the NATO aggression?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that this work of yours was financed by US government resources.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: In part.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In greater part or smaller part? Predominantly or negligibly so?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: The prior study to this was financed to my partners with US government funds, and this report was financed through funds to my partners with US government funds.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since you were not asked to study the flows of Serb refugees from Kosovo and Metohija, was it perhaps in your interest to compare in your statistical analysis, to do this at your own initiative?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of any figure related to the number of Serb refugees who left the area of Kosovo and Metohija during the bombing?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: I saw a paper presented at an international conference by a Serb statistician in September 2000 on this topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that this figure is about 100.000 Serbs who fled due to the intensive bombing of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: I do not know that. I do not recall the specifics from his presentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it your assessment that for the purposes of statistically analysing the data you have analysed here, it would have been useful for you to have taken into account these flows as well, related to Serbs and the non-Albanian population of Kosovo in general, and compared it to these flows?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: This study looks at refugee flow and killing against Kosovar Albanians. As such, it does not contain analysis of other groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you know very well that you are dealing with a complex issue related to a very complex conflict that was taking place in Kosovo and Metohija. Do you think that it is a considerable simplification or one-sided approach to have this boiled down to a statistical representation of figures pertaining to Albanian refugees only?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. There's a lot of parts to that question. I'm not sure I understood. Could you rephrase it for me? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In Kosovo, was this a complex conflict, a conflict that cannot be reduced only to one of its factors, that is to say, the statistical study of Albanian refugee flows?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: I'm not a political analyst, so I'm not -- I don't think I can answer whether this is complex. I have done a study of killings and refugee flows.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can studies be made about refugee flows if there are no elementary ideas about the historical, political, military, economic, social - and let me stop there - and any other context in which this analysis is sought to be made?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: This study examines the statistical patterns in light of three hypotheses, which I believe are the most important hypotheses that have been advanced to explain them. Neither I nor my co-authors are competent to make any additional analysis beyond the conclusions in this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who put these three hypotheses forth, the ones that you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: We took the hypotheses from political debates which we have heard expressed by different actors. Most locally to our work today, I have heard two of the hypotheses advanced by the accused in this case, and the other is in some sense advanced by my highly non-technical understanding of the indictment. So I believe they are relevant to our discussion today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to some of my hypotheses? Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then you misunderstood them, but we are going to get to that later. When presenting your C.V., when your C.V. was being presented, we heard that you had dealt in such statistics, in such statistical research, in a considerable number of countries over the past few years.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it possible to state that all the mentioned countries had crises, conflicts, and that the American administration was involved in all of these crises and conflicts?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL
utterances.text: Yes, all the countries had some sort of crisis or conflict. I don't think the involvement of the US government is clear in all of them. In some, it might be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And where was it not involved out of those that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What's the relevance of this, Mr. Milosevic, in relation to his evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, the relevance is in the fact that statistics that are well-known among the greatest statisticians of the world that can prove anything by statistics [as interpreted], and this is done to serve the purposes of the American politics aimed at enslavement. Chemistry is being misused for making chemical bombs, atomic energy for making atomic bombs --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... the witness. In the various -- just a moment. In the various studies that you were carrying out, were they in any way to serve the purposes of American politics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have never had, knowingly, contact with a representative of the US government in any of my work, in the sense that they would advance US interests through my work. However, I think there's a misconception, which may be helpful here, since my work in both El Salvador and Guatemala was actually quite critical of US interest and of US policy at the time. So this may help clarify the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll adjourn now. It's past half past 4.00. Would you be back tomorrow, please, half past 9.00, Dr. Ball.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 14th day of March 2002, at 9.30 a.m.
